chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 1 — Rome. A street
paragraphs: Enter a company of mutinous Citizens, with staves, clubs, and other weapons.
FIRST CITIZEN. Before we go any further, hear me speak.
ALL. Speak, speak!
FIRST CITIZEN. You'd all rather die than starve, is that right?
ALL. Yes, yes!
FIRST CITIZEN. First, you know Caius Martius is the people's chief enemy.
ALL. We know it, we know it!
FIRST CITIZEN. Let's kill him, and then we'll get grain at our own price. Is that agreed?
ALL. No more talk about it. Let's do it. Come on, come on!
SECOND CITIZEN. One word, good citizens.

FIRST CITIZEN. We're called the poor citizens, and the patricians the good ones. What they have too much of would feed us. If they gave us just their surplus while it was still fresh, we might think they were helping us out of kindness. But they think we cost too much. Our thinness, the sight of our misery, is like an inventory listing their wealth. Our suffering is their profit. Let's take revenge with our pikes before we become rakes, as thin as rakes. The gods know I say this out of hunger for bread, not thirst for revenge.
SECOND CITIZEN. Do you want to go especially against Caius Martius?
FIRST CITIZEN. Against him first. He's a real dog to the common people.
SECOND CITIZEN. Have you thought about what he's done for his country?
FIRST CITIZEN. Very well, and I'd be happy to speak well of him for it, except that he pays himself back by being proud.
SECOND CITIZEN. No, don't talk out of malice.

FIRST CITIZEN. I tell you, everything famous he's done, he did for that reason. Soft-hearted people are happy to say he did it for his country. He did it to please his mother and partly to be proud, which he is, as high as his courage goes.
SECOND CITIZEN. You call it a vice in him when he can't help his nature. You can't possibly say he's greedy.

FIRST CITIZEN. If I can't say that, I still don't run short of accusations. He has faults so many they'd tire us out to list. [_Shouts within_.] What are those shouts? The other side of the city has risen up. Why are we standing here chattering? To the Capitol!
ALL. Come on, come on!
Enter Menenius Agrippa.
FIRST CITIZEN. Wait, who's this coming?
SECOND CITIZEN. Worthy Menenius Agrippa, a man who has always loved the people.
FIRST CITIZEN. He's honest enough. I wish all the rest were!
MENENIUS. What are you up to, my countrymen? Where are you going with bats and clubs? What's the matter? Tell me, please.

FIRST CITIZEN. Our business is no secret to the Senate. They've had a hint for two weeks of what we mean to do, and now we'll show them in action. They say poor petitioners have strong breath. They'll find out we have strong arms too.
MENENIUS. Why, gentlemen, my good friends, my honest neighbors, will you destroy yourselves?
FIRST CITIZEN. We can't, sir. We're destroyed already.

MENENIUS. I tell you, friends, the patricians care for you with the greatest kindness. As for your needs and your suffering in this famine, you might as well strike at the heavens with your staves as lift them against the Roman state. Rome will go on its way and break ten thousand stronger chains than you could ever put in its path. As for the famine, the gods make it, not the patricians, and it's your knees to them that can help, not your arms. Alas, your misery has carried you off to a place where more trouble waits for you. And you slander the steersmen of the state, who care for you like fathers, when you curse them as enemies.

FIRST CITIZEN. Care for us? True, indeed! They've never cared for us yet. They let us starve while their storehouses are crammed with grain. They make laws to support moneylenders. They repeal, day after day, any good law passed against the rich, and every day they pass sharper laws to chain up and hold down the poor. If the wars don't eat us up, they will. That's all the love they bear us.

MENENIUS. Either you must admit you're terribly spiteful, or be accused of foolishness. I'll tell you a neat little story. Maybe you've heard it, but since it serves my purpose, I'll risk making it a little staler.
FIRST CITIZEN. Well, I'll hear it, sir. But don't think you can brush off our disgrace with a tale. Still, if you please, go ahead.

MENENIUS. There was a time when all the parts of the body rebelled against the belly, and accused it like this. It sat in the middle of the body like a pit, idle and doing nothing, always stuffing itself with food and never doing its share of work like the rest. Meanwhile the other organs saw and heard, planned, taught, walked, felt, and shared in serving the appetite and desires common to the whole body. The belly answered—
FIRST CITIZEN. Well, sir, what answer did the belly make?

MENENIUS. Sir, I'll tell you. It gave a kind of smile, not one that came from the lungs, but like this. (Look, I can make the belly smile as well as speak.) It replied in a mocking way to the discontented parts, the rebel members that envied what it took in. It was just the way you slander our senators because they aren't like you.

FIRST CITIZEN. Your belly's answer? What? The head with its royal crown, the watchful eye, the heart that gives counsel, the arm that's our soldier, the leg that's our horse, the tongue that's our trumpeter, with the other defenses and small helpers: this is our whole structure, and if they—
MENENIUS. What then? Upon my word, this fellow can talk. What then? What then?
FIRST CITIZEN. Should be held back by the greedy belly, which is the body's sewer—
MENENIUS. Well, what then?
FIRST CITIZEN. If those hard-working parts complained, what could the belly answer?
MENENIUS. I'll tell you, if you'll spare me a little patience, which is something you have little of. You'll hear the belly's answer.
FIRST CITIZEN. You're taking a long time about it.

MENENIUS. Mark this, good friend. Your most serious belly was deliberate, not rash like its accusers, and it answered like this: "It's true, my fellow members of the body," it said, "that I receive all the food first, the food you live on. And that's right, because I'm the storehouse and the shop of the whole body. But if you remember, I send it out through the rivers of your blood, even to the court, the heart, and to the seat of the brain. And through the twists and turns and offices of the body, the strongest nerves and the smallest veins receive from me the natural share they live on. And though all of you at once, my good friends"—this is what the belly says, mark me—
FIRST CITIZEN. Yes, sir, well, well.

MENENIUS. "Though all of you at once can't see what I hand out to each, yet I can make up my account and show that all of you get back from me the flour of everything, and leave me only the bran." What do you say to that?
FIRST CITIZEN. It was an answer. How do you apply it?

MENENIUS. The senators of Rome are this good belly, and you are the rebel members. Examine their counsels and their cares, and think it through properly, concerning the good of the commonwealth. You'll find no public benefit that you receive that doesn't come from them to you, and none at all from yourselves. What do you think, you, the big toe of this crowd?
FIRST CITIZEN. I, the big toe? Why the big toe?

MENENIUS. Because, being one of the lowest, meanest, poorest of this very wise rebellion, you go out in front. You rascal, you're the worst at running, yet you lead the way to grab some advantage. But get your stiff bats and clubs ready. Rome and her rats are about to fight, and one side must come to grief.
Enter Caius Martius.
Hail, noble Martius.
MARTIUS. Thanks.—What's the matter, you quarrelsome rogues? You scratch the poor itch of your opinions and turn yourselves into scabs.
FIRST CITIZEN. We always have your good word.

MARTIUS. Anyone who gives good words to you flatters at a disgusting level. What do you want, you curs, who like neither peace nor war? War frightens you, and peace makes you proud. Anyone who trusts you, where he should find lions, finds hares, and where he should find foxes, finds geese. You're no more reliable than a coal of fire on ice or a hailstone in the sun. Your idea of virtue is to make a man a hero when his crime has brought him down, and then to curse the justice that did it. Whoever deserves greatness deserves your hate. Your affections are a sick man's appetite, which wants most what will make his illness worse. Anyone who depends on your favors swims with fins of lead and cuts down oaks with reeds. Hang you! Trust you? Every minute you change your mind. You call him noble who was your hate a moment ago, and call him vile who was your garland. What's the matter, that in these different parts of the city you cry out against the noble Senate, which under the gods keeps you in awe, when otherwise you'd eat each other?—What are they after?
MENENIUS. Grain at their own price. They say the city is well stocked.

MARTIUS. Hang them! They say? They'll sit by the fire and presume to know what's being done in the Capitol, who's likely to rise, who's thriving and who's declining. They take sides in factions and spread rumors of marriages that are only guesses, making the parties they favor strong and leaving weak those they dislike, below their own cobbled shoes. They say there's grain enough? If the nobles would lay aside their pity and let me use my sword, I'd make a heap of these slaves, cut in quarters, as high as I could reach with my lance.
MENENIUS. No, these are almost completely persuaded. For though they have plenty of foolishness, they're extremely cowardly. But please, what does the other crowd say?

MARTIUS. They've broken up. Hang them! They said they were hungry. They sighed out proverbs: that hunger breaks stone walls, that dogs must eat, that meat was made for mouths, that the gods didn't send grain for rich men only. With these scraps they let out their complaints. When those were answered and they were granted a petition—a strange one, to break the heart of generosity and make bold power look pale—they threw their caps up as if they would hang them on the horns of the moon, shouting to outdo each other.
MENENIUS. What was granted them?

MARTIUS. Five tribunes to defend their common wisdom, of their own choosing. One is Junius Brutus, one Sicinius Velutus, and I don't know the rest. By God's death! The rabble should have pulled the roof off the city first before they got their way with me. In time this will win ground against power and throw up bigger subjects for rebellion to argue about.
MENENIUS. This is strange.
MARTIUS. Go home, you scraps.
Enter a Messenger hastily.
MESSENGER. Where's Caius Martius?
MARTIUS. Here. What's the matter?
MESSENGER. The news is, sir, the Volsces are in arms.
MARTIUS. I'm glad of it. Then we'll have a way to get rid of our moldy surplus.
Enter Sicinius Velutus, Junius Brutus, two Tribunes; Cominius, Titus Lartius with other Senators.
See, our best elders.
FIRST SENATOR. Martius, it's true, as you told us recently: the Volsces are in arms.
MARTIUS. They have a leader, Tullus Aufidius, who will test you. I sin in envying his nobility. If I were anything but what I am, I would wish to be only him.
COMINIUS. You have fought each other before.
MARTIUS. If half the world were fighting the other half and he were on my side, I'd change sides just to make my war only with him. He's a lion that I'm proud to hunt.
FIRST SENATOR. Then, worthy Martius, go with Cominius to these wars.
COMINIUS. It's what you promised before.
MARTIUS. Sir, it is, and I keep my word.—Titus Lartius, you'll see me strike at Tullus' face once more. What, are you stiff? Are you standing out?
TITUS LARTIUS. No, Caius Martius. I'll lean on one crutch and fight with the other before I'd stay behind from this business.
MENENIUS. Oh, well bred!
FIRST SENATOR. Come with us to the Capitol, where I know our greatest friends are waiting for us.
TITUS LARTIUS. Lead on. Follow Cominius. We must follow you. You deserve to go first.
COMINIUS. Noble Martius.
FIRST SENATOR.
[_To the Citizens_.]
Away to your homes, be gone.
MARTIUS. No, let them follow. The Volsces have a lot of grain. Take these rats there to gnaw at their granaries. Worshipful mutineers, your courage is budding nicely. Please follow.
[_Exeunt. Sicinius and Brutus remain_.]
SICINIUS. Was there ever a man as proud as this Martius?
BRUTUS. He has no equal.
SICINIUS. When we were chosen tribunes for the people—
BRUTUS. Did you notice his lip and eyes?
SICINIUS. No, his taunts.
BRUTUS. When he's angry, he won't hold back from jeering at the gods.
SICINIUS. He'd mock the modest moon.
BRUTUS. May the war devour him! He has grown too proud to be so brave.
SICINIUS. A nature like that, tickled by success, scorns even the shadow he steps on at noon. But I do wonder that his insolence can stand to be commanded under Cominius.

BRUTUS. The fame he aims at, and in which he already stands well, can't be better kept or more gained than by a place below the first. For whatever goes wrong will be the General's fault, though Martius does everything a man can. And fickle criticism will then cry out about Martius, "Oh, if he had run the business!"
SICINIUS. Besides, if things go well, the opinion that sticks so firmly to Martius will rob Cominius of what he really deserves.
BRUTUS. Come. Half of all Cominius' honors will go to Martius, though Martius didn't earn them. And all Martius' faults will be turned into honors, though in truth he deserves nothing in them.
SICINIUS. Let's go and hear how the dispatch is made, and how he goes into this present action, apart from his own singular way.
BRUTUS. Let's go.
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 2 — Corioles. The Senate House
paragraphs: Enter Tullus Aufidius with Senators of Corioles.
FIRST SENATOR. So, Aufidius, you think the Romans have got into our councils and know how we are proceeding.

AUFIDIUS. Don't you think so too? Has anything ever been planned in this state that could be turned into action before Rome had found a way to thwart it? It's not four days since I heard from there. These are the words. I think I have the letter here. Yes, here it is.
[_Reads_.] _They have raised an army, but it isn't known

whether for east or west. The famine is bad. The people are mutinous. And it is rumored that Cominius, Martius your old enemy (who is more hated in Rome than by you), and Titus Lartius, a very brave Roman, these three lead this force wherever it is aimed. Most likely it is for you. Think about it._
FIRST SENATOR. Our army is in the field. We never doubted that Rome was ready to meet us.

AUFIDIUS. And you didn't think it foolish to keep your great plans hidden until the time they had to show themselves. But it seems that while they were being hatched, Rome found out. Because of this discovery, our aim will fall short. It was to capture many towns before Rome even knew we were on the move.

SECOND SENATOR. Noble Aufidius, take your commission and hurry to your troops. Leave Corioles to us to guard. If they set up camp before us, bring up your army to drive them off. But I think you'll find they haven't prepared for us.

AUFIDIUS. Oh, don't doubt that. I speak from certainty. More than that, some parts of their forces are already out, and heading only this way. I leave your Honors now. If Caius Martius and I happen to meet, we have sworn we will keep striking until one of us can do no more.
ALL. The gods help you!
AUFIDIUS. And keep your Honors safe!
FIRST SENATOR. Farewell.
SECOND SENATOR. Farewell.
ALL. Farewell.
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 3 — Rome. An apartment in Martius’ house
paragraphs: Enter Volumnia and Virgilia, mother and wife to Martius. They set them down on two low stools and sew.

VOLUMNIA. Please, daughter, sing, or speak in a more cheerful way. If my son were my husband, I would rejoice more freely in his absence, when he won honor, than in the embraces of his bed, where he would show the most love. When he was still a tender boy, the only son of my womb, when youth and good looks drew every eye his way, when I wouldn't have sold an hour of seeing him for a whole day of kings' pleading, I thought about how honor would suit such a person. I thought that without fame to make it move, he was no better than a picture hanging on the wall. So I was glad to let him seek danger where he was likely to find fame. I sent him to a cruel war, and he came back with his brows wreathed in oak. I tell you, daughter, I didn't leap for joy more when I first heard I had a boy than I did when I first saw that he'd proved himself a man.
VIRGILIA. But if he had died in the fighting, madam, what then?

VOLUMNIA. Then his good reputation would have been my son. In it I would have found my offspring. Hear me say it honestly: if I had a dozen sons, each one loved equally, none less dear than yours and my good Martius, I would rather have eleven die nobly for their country than have one stuff himself in luxury and do nothing.
Enter a Gentlewoman.
GENTLEWOMAN. Madam, the Lady Valeria has come to visit you.
VIRGILIA. Please, let me go off by myself.

VOLUMNIA. Indeed you won't. I seem to hear your husband's drum here. I see him pull Aufidius down by the hair, with the Volsces fleeing from him the way children run from a bear. I seem to see him stamp his foot like this and shout like this: "Come on, you cowards! You were conceived in fear, though you were born in Rome." He wipes his bloody brow with his armored hand, and off he goes like a harvester who is given a job to mow it all or lose his pay.
VIRGILIA. His bloody brow? Oh Jupiter, no blood!

VOLUMNIA. Away, you fool! It suits a man better than a gilded trophy does. The breasts of Hecuba, when she nursed Hector, looked no lovelier than Hector's forehead when it spat out blood against a Greek sword, in defiance.—Tell Valeria we are ready to welcome her.
[_Exit Gentlewoman._]
VIRGILIA. Heavens protect my lord from fierce Aufidius!
VOLUMNIA. He'll beat Aufidius' head down below his knee and tread on his neck.
Enter Valeria with an Usher and a Gentlewoman.
VALERIA. My two ladies, good day to you.
VOLUMNIA. Sweet madam.
VIRGILIA. I'm glad to see your Ladyship.
VALERIA. How are you both? You're clearly stay-at-homes. What are you sewing here? A fine piece of work, truly. How is your little son?
VIRGILIA. I thank your Ladyship. He's well, good madam.
VOLUMNIA. He'd rather see swords and hear a drum than look at his schoolmaster.

VALERIA. On my word, his father's son! I swear he's a very pretty boy. On my faith, I watched him on Wednesday for half an hour straight. He has such a firm face. I saw him run after a gilded butterfly, and when he caught it, he let it go again, and ran after it again, and over and over he came, and got up again, and caught it again. Maybe his fall made him furious, or whatever it was, he clenched his teeth and tore it to bits. Oh, I swear, how he mangled it!
VOLUMNIA. One of his father's moods.
VALERIA. Indeed, yes, he's a noble child.
VIRGILIA. A rascal, madam.
VALERIA. Come, put away your needlework. I want you to play the idle housewife with me this afternoon.
VIRGILIA. No, good madam, I won't go out of doors.
VALERIA. Not out of doors?
VOLUMNIA. She will, she will.
VIRGILIA. Truly, no, with your permission. I won't cross the threshold until my lord returns from the wars.
VALERIA. Shame on you, you shut yourself in most unreasonably. Come, you must go visit the good lady who is in childbed.
VIRGILIA. I will wish her quick strength and visit her with my prayers, but I can't go there.
VOLUMNIA. Why, please?
VIRGILIA. It's not to save myself work, nor that I lack love.

VALERIA. You'd be another Penelope. Yet they say all the yarn she spun while Ulysses was away did nothing but fill Ithaca with moths. Come, I wish your cambric could feel like your finger, so you'd stop pricking it out of pity. Come, you shall go with us.
VIRGILIA. No, good madam, excuse me. Truly, I won't go out.
VALERIA. Truly, yes, go with me, and I'll tell you excellent news of your husband.
VIRGILIA. Oh, good madam, there can't be any yet.
VALERIA. Truly, I'm not joking with you. News came from him last night.
VIRGILIA. Really, madam!

VALERIA. In earnest, it's true. I heard a senator say it. This is how it is: the Volsces have an army out, and Cominius the General has gone against them with one part of our Roman forces. Your lord and Titus Lartius have camped before their city Corioles. They have no doubt of winning, and of making this a short war. This is true, on my honor, and so, please, come with us.
VIRGILIA. Give me an excuse, good madam. I'll obey you in everything from now on.
VOLUMNIA. Leave her alone, lady. As she is now, she'll only spoil our better mirth.
VALERIA. Truly, I think she would.—Farewell, then.—Come, good sweet lady.—Please, Virgilia, throw your solemnity out of doors, and come along with us.
VIRGILIA. No, in a word, madam. Truly I must not. I wish you much mirth.
VALERIA. Well then, farewell.
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 4 — Before Corioles
paragraphs: Enter Martius, Titus Lartius, with drum and colours, with Captains and Soldiers, as before the city of Corioles. To them a Messenger.
MARTIUS. News is coming there. I bet they have met.
LARTIUS. My horse against yours says no.
MARTIUS. Done.
LARTIUS. Agreed.
MARTIUS.
[_To Messenger_.] Tell me, has our general met the enemy?
MESSENGER. They lie in sight of each other but haven't spoken yet.
LARTIUS. So the good horse is mine.
MARTIUS. I'll buy him from you.
LARTIUS. No, I'll neither sell nor give him. I'll lend him to you for fifty years.—Summon the town.
MARTIUS. How far apart are these armies?
MESSENGER. Within a mile and a half.

MARTIUS. Then we'll hear their alarm, and they'll hear ours. Now, Mars, please make us quick at the work, so that with smoking swords we can march from here to help our friends in the field!—Come, blow your blast.
[_They sound a parley._]
Enter two Senators with others on the walls of Corioles.
Is Tullus Aufidius inside your walls?
FIRST SENATOR. No, and there's not a man who fears you less than he does. That's less than a little.
[_Drum afar off_.]

Listen, our drums are bringing out our young men. We'll break down our walls rather than let them shut us in. Our gates, which still look shut, are only fastened with reeds. They'll open by themselves.
[_Alarum far off_.]
Listen, far off! That's Aufidius. Hear what work he is making among your split army.
MARTIUS. Oh, they're at it!
LARTIUS. Their noise is our instruction.—Ladders, ho!
Enter the Army of the Volsces as through the city gates.

MARTIUS. They don't fear us but come out of their city.—Now put your shields in front of your hearts, and fight with hearts tougher than shields.—Advance, brave Titus. They scorn us far more than I thought, and that makes me sweat with rage.—Come on, my fellows! Whoever retreats, I'll take him for a Volsce, and he'll feel my edge.
[_Alarums. The Romans are beat back to their trenches. They exit, with the Volsces following_.]
Enter Martius cursing, with Roman soldiers.

MARTIUS. May all the infections of the south fall on you, you shames of Rome! You herd of—Boils and plagues cover you all over, so that you are hated farther than you can be seen, and one of you infects another a mile away against the wind! You souls of geese, who wear the shapes of men, how you ran from slaves that apes would beat! By Pluto and hell! All wounded in the back. Backs red, and faces pale with flight and shivering fear! Mend yourselves and charge home, or, by the fires of heaven, I'll leave the enemy and make my wars on you. Watch yourselves. Come on! If you'll stand firm, we'll beat them back to their wives, as they beat us back to our trenches. Follow me!
[_Another alarum. The Volsces re-enter and are driven back to the gates of Corioles, which open to admit them._]
So, now the gates are open. Now prove good seconds! Fortune opens them for those who follow, not for those who flee. Watch me, and do the same.
[_Martius follows the fleeing Volsces through the gates, and is shut in._]
FIRST SOLDIER. Foolhardiness, not me.
SECOND SOLDIER. Not me either.
FIRST SOLDIER. Look, they've shut him in.
[_Alarum continues._]
ALL. He's in the stew pot, I'll bet.
Enter Titus Lartius.
LARTIUS. What has become of Martius?
ALL. Slain, sir, without a doubt.
FIRST SOLDIER. He followed the fleeing men at their very heels and went in with them. They suddenly slammed their gates shut. He is alone, to answer the whole city.

LARTIUS. Oh noble fellow, who feels the pain and still outdares his own senseless sword, and when it bends, stands up! You are lost, Martius. A whole carbuncle as big as you are would not be so rich a jewel. You were a soldier to Cato's wish, not only fierce and terrible in your strokes, but with your grim looks and the thunderlike force of your voice you made your enemies shake, as if the world were feverish and trembling.
Enter Martius, bleeding, assaulted by the enemy.
FIRST SOLDIER. Look, sir.
LARTIUS. Oh, it's Martius! Let's fetch him out or stay with him in the same fate.
[_They fight, and all enter the city._]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 5 — Within Corioles. A street
paragraphs: Enter certain Romans, with spoils.
FIRST ROMAN. I'll carry this to Rome.
SECOND ROMAN. And I'll take this.
THIRD ROMAN. A plague on it! I thought this was silver.
Enter Martius and Titus Lartius with a Trumpet.

MARTIUS. Look at these scavengers, who value their hours at a cracked drachma. Cushions, lead spoons, irons worth a doit, the smallest coin, doublets that hangmen would bury with the men who wore them. These base slaves pack up their loot before the fight is even over. Down with them!
[_Exit the Romans with spoils._]
[_Alarum continues still afar off._]

And listen, what a noise the General is making! Go to him! There is Aufidius, the man my soul hates, cutting through our Romans. So, valiant Titus, take enough men to hold the city, while I, with those who have the spirit, hurry to help Cominius.
LARTIUS. Worthy sir, you're bleeding. Your exertion has been too violent for a second round of fighting.
MARTIUS. Sir, don't praise me. My work hasn't even warmed me yet. Farewell. The blood I'm losing is more like medicine than a danger to me. This is how I'll appear to Aufidius and fight him.
LARTIUS. Now may the fair goddess Fortune fall deeply in love with you, and may her great charms send your opponents' swords astray! Bold gentleman, may Prosperity be your page!
MARTIUS. May she be as much your friend as she is to those she places highest! So, farewell.
LARTIUS. You worthiest Martius!
[_Exit Martius._]
Go sound your trumpet in the marketplace. Call there all the officers of the town, where they will learn what we intend. Go!
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 6 — Near the camp of Cominius
paragraphs: Enter Cominius as it were in retire, with Soldiers.

COMINIUS. Catch your breath, my friends. Well fought! We've come off like Romans, neither foolish in standing our ground nor cowardly in retreating. Believe me, sirs, we'll be attacked again. While we were striking, we heard now and then, between blows and on gusts of wind, the attacks of our friends. May the Roman gods lead their successes as we wish them to lead our own, so that both our armies, meeting with smiling faces, may give you thankful sacrifice!
Enter a Messenger.
What's your news?
MESSENGER. The citizens of Corioles have come out and given battle to Lartius and Martius. I saw our side driven back to their trenches, and then I came away.
COMINIUS. Though you speak the truth, I think you don't speak well. How long ago was that?
MESSENGER. More than an hour, my lord.
COMINIUS. It's not a mile away. We heard their drums a short while ago. How could you mix up an hour in a mile and bring your news so late?
MESSENGER. Volscian spies chased me, so I was forced to circle three or four miles around. Otherwise, sir, I would have brought my report half an hour ago.
[_Exit Messenger._]
Enter Martius, bloody.
COMINIUS. Who's that over there, who looks as if he'd been flayed? Oh gods, he has the stamp of Martius, and I have seen him like this before.
MARTIUS. Do I come too late?
COMINIUS. A shepherd can no more mistake thunder for a tabor than I can mistake the sound of Martius' voice for that of any lesser man.
MARTIUS. Do I come too late?
COMINIUS. Yes, if you don't come in the blood of others but wrapped in your own.
MARTIUS. Oh, let me embrace you in arms as sound as when I courted, and with a heart as merry as when our wedding day was done and the candles burned toward bed!
COMINIUS. Flower of warriors, how is it with Titus Lartius?

MARTIUS. Like a man busy with decrees, condemning some to death and some to exile, ransoming one man or pitying him, threatening another. He holds Corioles in the name of Rome like a fawning greyhound on a leash, to let it slip whenever he likes.
COMINIUS. Where is that slave who told me they had beaten you back to your trenches? Where is he? Call him here.

MARTIUS. Leave him alone. He told the truth. But as for our gentlemen, the common rank and file—a plague on them! Tribunes for them!—the mouse never ran from the cat as they did run from rascals worse than themselves.
COMINIUS. But how did you win?
MARTIUS. Is there time to tell it? I don't think so. Where is the enemy? Are you lords of the field? If not, why do you stop until you are?
COMINIUS. Martius, we fought at a disadvantage, and we retreated to achieve our purpose.
MARTIUS. How does their battle line lie? Do you know on which side they've placed their trusted men?
COMINIUS. As I guess, Martius, their troops in the front line are the Antiates, the ones they trust most. Over them is Aufidius, the very heart of their hope.

MARTIUS. I beg you, by all the battles in which we have fought, by the blood we have shed together, by the vows we have made to stay friends, that you set me right away against Aufidius and his Antiates. And don't put off the moment. Fill the air with raised swords and darts, and let us put it to the test this very hour.
COMINIUS. Though I could wish you were taken to a gentle bath and had balms put on you, still I dare never refuse your request. Take your pick of those who can best help your action.

MARTIUS. Those are the ones who are most willing. If any such are here—and it would be a sin to doubt it—who love this paint I'm smeared with, which you see on me. If any fear for their person less than for a bad reputation. If any think a brave death outweighs a bad life, and that their country is dearer than themselves. Let him alone, or as many so minded, wave like this to show his disposition and follow Martius.
[_He waves his sword._]
[_They all shout and wave their swords, take him up in their arms, and cast up their caps._]

Oh, me alone! Do you make a sword of me? If these shows aren't only on the outside, which of you isn't worth four Volsces? Not one of you who can't carry against the great Aufidius a shield as hard as his. Though I thank you all, I must choose a certain number from among you all. The rest will take on the business in some other fight, as the need demands. Please march, and I'll quickly pick out my force, whichever men are most willing.
COMINIUS. March on, my fellows. Make good this show, and you will share in everything with us.
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 7 — The gates of Corioles
paragraphs: Titus Lartius, having set a guard upon Corioles, going with drum and trumpet toward Cominius and Caius Martius, enters with a Lieutenant, other Soldiers, and a Scout.

LARTIUS. So, let the gates be guarded. Keep to your duties as I have set them down. If I send word, dispatch those companies of a hundred to our aid. The rest will do for a short defense. If we lose the field, we can't keep the town.
LIEUTENANT. Don't worry about our care, sir.
LARTIUS. Go, and shut your gates behind us. Our guide, come. Take us to the Roman camp.
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 8 — A field of battle between the Roman and the Volscian camps
paragraphs: Alarum, as in battle. Enter Martius and Aufidius at several doors.
MARTIUS. I'll fight no one but you, for I hate you worse than a promise-breaker.
AUFIDIUS. We hate alike. Africa has no serpent I loathe more than your fame and your envy. Plant your foot.
MARTIUS. Let the first to budge die as the other's slave, and may the gods damn him afterward!
AUFIDIUS. If I run, Martius, hoot at me like a hare.

MARTIUS. Within these three hours, Tullus, I fought alone inside the walls of your Corioles, and did whatever I pleased there. It's not my blood that you see me masked in. For your revenge, wrench up your strength to the highest.
AUFIDIUS. Even if you were the Hector who was the whip of your bragged-about ancestors, you wouldn't escape me here.
[_Here they fight, and certain Volsces come to the aid of Aufidius._]
Meddling and not brave, you have shamed me with your damned help.
[_Martius fights till they be driven in breathless. Aufidius and Martius exit, separately._]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 9 — The Roman camp
paragraphs: Alarum. A retreat is sounded. Flourish. Enter, at one door, Cominius with the Romans; at another door, Martius, with his arm in a scarf.

COMINIUS. If I were to tell you over today's work, you wouldn't believe your own deeds. But I'll report it where senators will mix tears with smiles. Great patricians will listen and shrug, and in the end admire. Ladies will be frightened, and gladly trembling, will hear more. And the dull tribunes, who with the musty plebeians hate your honors, will say against their hearts, "We thank the gods that Rome has such a soldier." Yet you came to only a morsel of this feast, having dined fully before.
Enter Titus Lartius with his power, from the pursuit.
LARTIUS. Oh general, here is the steed, and we are only the trappings. If you had seen—

MARTIUS. Please, no more. My mother, who has a license to praise her own blood, grieves me when she praises me. I have done what you have done, and that's all I can do. I was driven as you were, and that's for my country. Anyone who has only carried out his good will has outdone my action.

COMINIUS. You shall not be the grave of your own deserving. Rome must know the value of her own. It would be a concealment worse than theft, no less than slander, to hide your deeds and to silence what, praised to the spire and top of praise, would still seem modest. Therefore, I beg you, as a sign of what you are, not as a reward for what you have done, to hear me before our army.
MARTIUS. I have some wounds on me, and they smart to hear themselves remembered.

COMINIUS. If they didn't, they might well fester against ingratitude and dress themselves with death. Of all the horses, of which we have taken a good and large store, and of all the treasure won in this field and city, we give you the tenth part, to be taken out before the common division, at your sole choice.
MARTIUS. I thank you, general, but I can't make my heart agree to take a bribe to pay my sword. I refuse it, and I stand on my common share with those who have seen the doing.
[_A long flourish. They all cry “Martius, Martius!” and cast up their caps and lances. Cominius and Lartius stand bare._]

May these same instruments, which you profane, never sound again! When drums and trumpets prove flatterers in the field, let courts and cities be made all of false-faced flattery! When steel grows soft, as soft as the parasite's silk, let him be made a cheering man for the wars! No more, I say. Because I haven't washed my nose that bled, or beaten some feeble wretch (which many others here have done without notice), you shout me out in exaggerated cheers, as if I loved having my little deed fed on praises sauced with lies.

COMINIUS. You are too modest, more cruel to your good reputation than grateful to us who give it to you truly. With your patience, if you are angry against yourself, we'll put you in manacles, like one who means to do himself harm, and then reason with you safely. Therefore let it be known, to the whole world as to us, that Caius Martius wears this war's garland. As a token of it, I give him my noble steed, known to the camp, with all his fittings. And from this time, for what he did before Corioles, call him, with all the applause and clamor of the army, Caius Martius Coriolanus! Bear the added name nobly always!
[_Flourish. Trumpets sound, and drums._]
ALL. Caius Martius Coriolanus!

CORIOLANUS. I will go wash, and when my face is clean, you'll see whether I blush or not. However, I thank you. I mean to ride your steed and to live up, at all times, to the good name you've added, as far as my strength allows.

COMINIUS. So, to our tent, where, before we rest, we will write to Rome about our success.—You, Titus Lartius, must go back to Corioles. Send us to Rome the best men, with whom we may draw up terms for their good and ours.
LARTIUS. I will, my lord.
CORIOLANUS. The gods begin to mock me. I, who just now refused the most princely gifts, am bound to beg from my lord general.
COMINIUS. Take it, it's yours. What is it?

CORIOLANUS. I once lodged here in Corioles at a poor man's house, and he treated me kindly. He cried out to me, and I saw him a prisoner. But then Aufidius came into my view, and rage overwhelmed my pity. I ask you to give my poor host his freedom.
COMINIUS. Oh, well begged! Even if he were the butcher of my son, he would be as free as the wind.—Release him, Titus.
LARTIUS. Martius, his name?
CORIOLANUS. By Jupiter, I've forgotten! I'm weary. Yes, my memory is tired. Don't we have any wine here?
COMINIUS. Let's go to our tent. The blood on your face is drying. It's time it was looked after. Come.
[_A flourish of cornets. Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 10 — The camp of the Volsces
paragraphs: A flourish. Cornets. Enter Tullus Aufidius, bloody, with two or three soldiers.
AUFIDIUS. The town has been taken.
SOLDIER. It will be handed back on fair terms.

AUFIDIUS. Terms? I wish I were a Roman, because as a Volsce I can't be what I am. Terms? What good terms can a treaty offer to the side that's at the winner's mercy? Five times, Martius, I have fought you, and five times you have beaten me. I think you'd keep doing it if we met as often as we eat. By the elements, if I ever meet him face to face again, either he's mine or I'm his. My rivalry has lost the honor it once had. I used to hope to crush him with equal force, true sword against true sword. Now I'll stab at him any way I can, whether rage or cunning gets him.
SOLDIER. He's the devil.

AUFIDIUS. He's bolder, though not as sly. My courage has been poisoned, stained only by what I've suffered from him. Because of him it will fly out of its own nature. Neither sleep nor sanctuary will hold me back, whether he is naked, sick, in a temple or at the Capitol. Priests' prayers and times of sacrifice are all barriers to my fury, and none of their rotten privilege and custom will stand against my hatred of Martius. Wherever I find him, even at home under my brother's protection, even there, against the law of hospitality, I would wash my fierce hand in his heart. Go into the city. Find out how it's held, and who the hostages for Rome must be.
SOLDIER. Won't you go yourself?
AUFIDIUS. I'm expected at the cypress grove. Please, it's south of the city mills. Bring me word there of how things stand, so I can quicken my journey to match.
SOLDIER. I will, sir.
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 1 — Rome. A public place
paragraphs: Enter Menenius with the two Tribunes of the people, Sicinius and Brutus.
MENENIUS. The augurer tells me we'll have news tonight.
BRUTUS. Good or bad?
MENENIUS. Not what the people are praying for, because they don't love Martius.
SICINIUS. Nature teaches animals to know their friends.
MENENIUS. Tell me, who does the wolf love?
SICINIUS. The lamb.
MENENIUS. Yes, to devour him, just as the hungry plebeians would devour the noble Martius.
BRUTUS. He's a lamb indeed, who bleats like a bear.
MENENIUS. He's a bear indeed, who lives like a lamb. You two are old men. Tell me one thing I'm going to ask you.
BOTH TRIBUNES. Well, sir?
MENENIUS. What great fault is Martius short of, that you two don't have plenty of?
BRUTUS. He's short of no single fault. He's stocked with all of them.
SICINIUS. Especially pride.
BRUTUS. And above all the rest, boasting.
MENENIUS. That's strange. Do you two know what people think of you here in the city? I mean those of us on the right-hand side, the patricians. Do you?
BOTH TRIBUNES. Why, what do they think of us?
MENENIUS. Since you've been talking about pride, won't you lose your tempers?
BOTH TRIBUNES. Come on, sir, out with it.

MENENIUS. Why, it's no great matter. A tiny thief of an occasion will rob you of a great deal of patience. Give your tempers free rein and be angry as much as you please, at least if you find any pleasure in being angry. You blame Martius for being proud.
BRUTUS. We're not the only ones who do, sir.

MENENIUS. I know you can do very little alone. Your helpers are many, or else your actions would be very lonely. Your abilities are too childish to do much alone. You talk of pride. Oh, if only you could turn your eyes to the backs of your own necks and take a look inside your fine selves! Oh, if only you could!
BOTH TRIBUNES. What then, sir?
MENENIUS. Why, then you'd discover a pair of undeserving, proud, violent, touchy magistrates, otherwise known as fools, as bad as any in Rome.
SICINIUS. Menenius, you're known well enough yourself.

MENENIUS. I'm known as a moody patrician who loves a cup of hot wine without a drop of watery Tiber in it. They say I'm a bit flawed in favoring the first side who complains, and that I'm hasty and flare up like tinder at the slightest push. I spend more time with the backside of the night than with the forehead of the morning. What I think, I say, and I spend my spite in my breath. When I meet two such public servants as you, and I can't call you Lycurguses, if the drink you hand me offends my palate, I pull a sour face at it. I can't say your Worships have handled the matter well when I find the ass mixed into most of your words. I'll have to put up with those who say you're respectable, serious men, but anyone who tells you that you have good faces is lying badly. If you can see all this in the map of my little world, does it follow that I'm known well enough? What harm can your half-blind stares gather out of this portrait, if I'm known well enough?
BRUTUS. Come, sir, come. We know you well enough.

MENENIUS. You know neither me, nor yourselves, nor anything. You're ambitious for the caps and bows of poor wretches. You wear out a good healthy morning hearing a case between an orange-seller and a tap-seller, and then you postpone the dispute over threepence to another day of hearings. When you're hearing a case between two parties, if you happen to get a pang of colic, you pull faces like actors in a mime, raise the bloody flag against all patience, and, roaring for a chamber pot, send the dispute away bleeding, more tangled than before you heard it. All the peace you make in their cause is calling both parties knaves. You're a strange pair.
BRUTUS. Come, come. Everyone understands you're better as a jester at the dinner table than as a useful bench-sitter in the Capitol.

MENENIUS. Even our priests would have to turn into mockers if they met such ridiculous subjects as you. When you speak your best and most to the point, it isn't worth the wagging of your beards. And your beards don't deserve so honorable a grave as stuffing a patcher's cushion or being buried in an ass's packsaddle. Yet you must go on saying Martius is proud, when at a cheap estimate he's worth all your predecessors since Deucalion, though perhaps the best of them were hereditary hangmen. Good evening to your Worships. More of your company would infect my brain, you herdsmen of the beastly plebeians. I'll be bold and take my leave of you.
[_He begins to exit. Brutus and Sicinius stand aside._]
Enter Volumnia, Virgilia and Valeria
How are you, my ladies, as fair as you are noble, and the moon herself, if she were earthly, would be no nobler? Where are you hurrying off to, following your eyes so fast?
VOLUMNIA. Honorable Menenius, my boy Martius is coming. For the love of Juno, let's go!
MENENIUS. Ha? Martius coming home?
VOLUMNIA. Yes, worthy Menenius, and with the highest approval.
MENENIUS. Take my cap, Jupiter, and thank you! Hoo! Martius coming home?
VALERIA, VIRGILIA. No, it's true.
VOLUMNIA. Look, here's a letter from him. The state has another, his wife has another, and I think there's one at home for you.
MENENIUS. I'll make my very house shake tonight. A letter for me?
VIRGILIA. Yes, certainly, there's a letter for you. I saw it.

MENENIUS. A letter for me? It gives me seven years of good health, and in that time I'll stick my lip out at the doctor. The best prescription in Galen is only quackery, and next to this tonic it's no better than a horse's drench. Isn't he wounded? He used to come home wounded.
VIRGILIA. Oh, no, no, no!
VOLUMNIA. Oh, he is wounded, and I thank the gods for it.
MENENIUS. So do I too, if it isn't too much. If he brings victory in his pocket, the wounds suit him.
VOLUMNIA. On his brows, Menenius. He comes home for the third time with the oak garland.
MENENIUS. Has he given Aufidius a thorough beating?
VOLUMNIA. Titus Lartius writes that they fought face to face, but Aufidius got away.

MENENIUS. And it was time for him to go, I'll vouch for that. If he had stayed with Martius, I wouldn't have wanted to be 'fidiused like that for all the chests in Corioles and the gold that's in them. Does the Senate know about this?

VOLUMNIA. Good ladies, let's go. Yes, yes, yes. The Senate has letters from the General, in which he gives my son the whole credit for the war. In this action he has outdone his former deeds twice over.
VALERIA. Truly, wonderful things are said about him.
MENENIUS. Wonderful? Yes, I assure you, and not without his having truly earned them.
VIRGILIA. May the gods make them true.
VOLUMNIA. True? Pooh, nonsense!
MENENIUS. True? I'll swear they are true. Where is he wounded? [_To the Tribunes_.] God save your good Worships! Martius is coming home. He has more reason than ever to be proud. Where is he wounded?

VOLUMNIA. In the shoulder and the left arm. There will be large scars to show the people when he stands for his place as consul. He received seven wounds in his body in the fight that drove Tarquin back.
MENENIUS. One in the neck and two in the thigh. That makes nine that I know of.
VOLUMNIA. Before this last expedition he had twenty-five wounds on him.
MENENIUS. Now it's twenty-seven. Every gash was an enemy's grave.
[_A shout and flourish_.]
Listen, the trumpets!
VOLUMNIA. These are Martius's heralds. Before him he carries noise, and behind him he leaves tears. Death, that dark spirit, lies in his sinewy arm. When it's raised, it comes down, and then men die.
[_A sennet_.]
Enter Cominius the General and Titus Lartius, between them Coriolanus crowned with an oaken garland, with Captains and Soldiers and a Herald. Trumpets sound.

HERALD. Know, Rome, that Martius fought all alone within the gates of Corioles. There he won glory, and with it a new name added to Caius Martius. In honor of that, the name "Coriolanus" follows. Welcome to Rome, renowned Coriolanus.
[_Sound flourish._]
ALL. Welcome to Rome, renowned Coriolanus!
CORIOLANUS. No more of this, it hurts my heart. Please, no more.
COMINIUS. Look, sir, your mother.
CORIOLANUS. Oh, I know you have prayed to all the gods for my success.
[_Kneels._]
VOLUMNIA. No, my good soldier, stand up.
[_He stands._]
My gentle Martius, worthy Caius, newly named by honor won through deeds. What is it? Must I call you Coriolanus? But oh, your wife.

CORIOLANUS. My gracious silence, hello. Would you have laughed if I'd come home in a coffin, since you weep to see me triumph? Ah, my dear, those are the eyes the widows in Corioles wear, and the mothers who lack sons.
MENENIUS. Now may the gods crown you!
CORIOLANUS. And are you still alive? [_To Valeria_] Oh, my sweet lady, forgive me.
VOLUMNIA. I don't know where to turn. Oh, welcome home! And welcome, General. And you're all welcome.

MENENIUS. A hundred thousand welcomes! I could weep and I could laugh. I feel light and heavy at once. Welcome. May a curse strike at the very root of the heart of anyone who isn't glad to see you! You three are what Rome should dote on. Yet, on my word, we have some old crab-apple trees here at home that can't be grafted to suit your taste. But welcome, warriors! We call a nettle just a nettle, and the faults of fools just folly.
COMINIUS. Always right.
CORIOLANUS. Menenius, always, always.
HERALD. Make way there, and move on!
CORIOLANUS.
[_To Volumnia and Virgilia_.] Your hand, and yours.
Before I go under my own roof, I must visit the good patricians. I've received not only greetings from them but new honors with them.
VOLUMNIA. I have lived to see my very wishes fulfilled and the castles of my imagination built. Only one thing is still missing, and I don't doubt Rome will put it on you.
CORIOLANUS. Know this, good mother. I would rather serve them in my own way than rule with them in theirs.
COMINIUS. On, to the Capitol.
[_Flourish of cornets. Exeunt in state, as before._]
Brutus and Sicinius come forward.

BRUTUS. Every tongue speaks of him, and bleary eyes put on spectacles to see him. Your chattering nurse lets her baby cry in a rapture while she chats about him. The kitchen maid pins her best linen round her greasy neck and climbs the walls to get a look at him. Stalls, shop-fronts and windows are crammed, rooftops are full, and ridges are straddled by people of every sort, all agreeing in their eagerness to see him. Priests who are seldom seen push into the common crowds and puff to win a place among the vulgar. Our veiled ladies leave the battle of white and rose in their carefully painted cheeks to the wanton spoiling of the sun's burning kisses. All this fuss, as if whichever god leads him had slyly crept into his human powers and given him his graceful bearing.
SICINIUS. I'll bet he's made consul right away.
BRUTUS. Then our office may go to sleep for as long as he's in power.
SICINIUS. He can't carry his honors with moderation from where he should begin to where he should end. He'll lose the ones he has won.
BRUTUS. There's comfort in that.

SICINIUS. Don't doubt the commoners we represent. With their old malice they'll forget these new honors of his at the slightest cause. And as for him giving them that cause, don't doubt it, as surely as he is proud to do it.

BRUTUS. I heard him swear that if he stood for consul he'd never appear in the marketplace, nor put on the threadbare gown of humility, nor show his wounds to the people as the custom is, and beg for their stinking breaths.
SICINIUS. That's right.
BRUTUS. Those were his words. Oh, he'd rather go without the office than win it any way except by the gentry begging him and the nobles wanting it.
SICINIUS. I wish nothing better than that he keeps that purpose and carries it out.
BRUTUS. He most likely will.
SICINIUS. Then it will be, to him, as we hope, certain destruction.

BRUTUS. So it must turn out, either for him or for our authority, once and for all. We must suggest to the people how much he has always hated them. As far as he could, he would have made them mules, silenced their spokesmen, and stripped them of their freedoms. He considers them, in human action and capacity, to have no more soul or fitness for the world than camels in war, which are fed only to carry burdens and get hard blows for collapsing under them.

SICINIUS. As you say, once this is suggested to them, at some moment when his soaring insolence offends the people, it will be his fire to light their dry stubble. That moment won't be lacking if it's pushed, and that's as easy as setting dogs on sheep. Their blaze will darken him forever.
Enter a Messenger.
BRUTUS. What's the matter?

MESSENGER. You're sent for to the Capitol. It's thought Martius will be consul. I have seen the dumb throng to see him and the blind to hear him speak. Matrons flung gloves, and ladies and girls flung scarves and handkerchiefs, at him as he passed. The nobles bowed as to Jove's statue, and the commoners made a shower and thunder with their caps and shouts. I never saw the like.
BRUTUS. Let's go to the Capitol, and bring ears and eyes for the moment, but hearts for what comes of it.
SICINIUS. I'm with you.
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 2 — Rome. The Capitol
paragraphs: Enter two Officers, to lay cushions, as it were in the Capitol.
FIRST OFFICER. Come, come. They're almost here. How many are standing for consul?
SECOND OFFICER. Three, they say, but everyone thinks Coriolanus will win it.
FIRST OFFICER. He's a brave fellow, but he's terribly proud and doesn't love the common people.

SECOND OFFICER. Honestly, many great men have flattered the people without ever loving them. And there are many the people have loved without knowing why. So if they love without knowing why, they hate on no better ground. Therefore Coriolanus's not caring whether they love or hate him shows how well he understands their nature. In his noble carelessness he lets them see it plainly.

FIRST OFFICER. If he didn't care whether he had their love or not, he would hover indifferently between doing them neither good nor harm. But he seeks their hatred with more devotion than they can give him, and leaves nothing undone that might fully show him to be their opposite. Now, to seem to go after the people's malice and displeasure is as bad as what he dislikes, flattering them for their love.

SECOND OFFICER. He has deserved well of his country. His rise has not come by such easy steps as those who were gracious and polite to the people, doffing their caps, without any further deed to win a place in their esteem and talk. He has planted his honors so firmly in their eyes and his actions in their hearts that for their tongues to be silent and not admit so much would be a kind of ungrateful injury. To say otherwise would be a malice that, giving itself the lie, would draw reproof and rebuke from every ear that heard it.
FIRST OFFICER. No more about him. He's a worthy man. Make way. They're coming.

A sennet. Enter the Patricians and the Tribunes of the people, Lictors before them; Coriolanus, Menenius, Cominius the consul. The Patricians sit.  Sicinius and Brutus take their places by themselves. Coriolanus stands.

MENENIUS. We have settled the matter of the Volsces and decided to send for Titus Lartius. What remains, as the main point of this later meeting, is to reward the noble service of the man who has stood up for his country like this. So may it please you, most reverend and grave elders, to ask the present consul, who was also the last general, to report a little, on our well-found successes, of that worthy work done by Martius Caius Coriolanus. We have met here both to thank him and to honor him with honors worthy of himself.
[_Coriolanus sits._]

FIRST SENATOR. Speak, good Cominius. Leave nothing out for the sake of length. Make us think our state is short of means to repay him, rather than that we are stretching it out. Masters of the people, we ask for your kindest ears, and afterward your loving urging toward the common body to agree to what passes here.
SICINIUS. We have come together for a pleasing negotiation, and our hearts are inclined to honor and advance the subject of our assembly.
BRUTUS. We'll be all the happier to do so if he remembers to put a kinder value on the people than he has so far.
MENENIUS. That's off the point, that's off the point! I wish you had kept quiet. Would you like to hear Cominius speak?
BRUTUS. Very willingly. But my caution was more to the point than the rebuke you give it.
MENENIUS. He loves your people, but don't tie him down to being their bedfellow. Worthy Cominius, speak.
[_Coriolanus rises, and offers to go away._]
No, keep your place.
FIRST SENATOR. Sit, Coriolanus. Never be ashamed to hear what you have nobly done.
CORIOLANUS. Your Honors, pardon me. I would rather have my wounds heal again than hear how I got them.
BRUTUS. Sir, I hope my words didn't drive you from your seat?
CORIOLANUS. No, sir. Yet often, when blows have made me stay, I have fled from words. You didn't flatter me, so you didn't hurt me. But your people, I love them for what they weigh.
MENENIUS. Please, sit down.
CORIOLANUS. I would rather have someone scratch my head in the sun when the alarm was sounded than sit idly here to hear my nothings made into monsters.
[_Exit._]

MENENIUS. Masters of the people, how can he flatter your multiplying spawn, when you see he would rather risk all his limbs for honor than hear it with one of his ears? And that's a thousand to one good one. Go on, Cominius.

COMINIUS. My voice will fall short. The deeds of Coriolanus should not be spoken of feebly. It's held that courage is the chief virtue and most dignifies the one who has it. If that's so, the man I speak of can't be matched by any single man in the world. At sixteen, when Tarquin raised an army against Rome, he fought beyond what anyone else did. Our dictator then, whom I name with all praise, saw him fight when he drove the bristled lips before him with his Amazon's beardless chin. He stood over a fallen Roman and, in the Consul's view, killed three opponents. He met Tarquin himself and struck him to his knees. In the feats of that day, when he might have played the woman in the play, he proved the best man in the field. For his reward he was crowned with the oak. Having entered manhood this way in his youth, he grew like a sea. In the heat of seventeen battles since, he has carried off the garland from all swords. As for this last action, before and in Corioles, let me say I can't do him justice. He stopped the runaways, and by his rare example he turned cowards' terror into sport. As weeds give way before a ship under sail, so men obeyed and fell below his prow. His sword, Death's stamp, took whatever it marked. From face to foot he was a thing of blood, and his every movement was timed to dying cries. Alone he entered the deadly gate of the city, which he painted with unavoidable doom. Alone he came out, and with a sudden reinforcement struck Corioles like a planet. Now it was all his, when soon the din of war pierced his ready senses. Then at once his doubled spirit revived what was worn out in his flesh, and he went to the battle. There he ran dripping over men's lives as if it were endless plunder. Until we could call both field and city ours, he never stopped to ease his breast with panting.
MENENIUS. Worthy man!
FIRST SENATOR. He can't help but match the honors we devise for him.

COMINIUS. He kicked at our spoils and looked at precious things as if they were the common muck of the world. He wants less than misery itself would give. He rewards his deeds by doing them, and is content to spend his time just getting it done.
MENENIUS. He's truly noble. Let him be called for.
FIRST SENATOR. Call Coriolanus.
OFFICER. He's here.
Enter Coriolanus.
MENENIUS. The Senate, Coriolanus, is well pleased to make you consul.
CORIOLANUS. I still owe them my life and services.
MENENIUS. Then what remains is that you speak to the people.
CORIOLANUS. I beg you, let me skip that custom. I can't put on the gown, stand there exposed, and beg them to give their votes for the sake of my wounds. Please let me pass over this.
SICINIUS. Sir, the people must have their votes, and they won't give up one bit of ceremony.
MENENIUS. Don't push them to it. Please go and fit yourself to the custom, and take your honor with the proper form, as your predecessors have.
CORIOLANUS. It is a part I'd blush to act, and it might well be taken away from the people.
BRUTUS. Did you hear that?
CORIOLANUS. To brag to them, "Thus I did, and thus!" To show them the scars that no longer ache, which I should hide, as if I had received them as payment for their breath alone!
MENENIUS. Don't insist on it. We hand to you, tribunes of the people, our proposal to them, and to our noble consul we wish all joy and honor.
SENATORS. To Coriolanus come all joy and honor!
[_Flourish cornets. Exeunt all but Sicinius and Brutus._]
BRUTUS. You see how he intends to treat the people.
SICINIUS. May they see his intent! He will ask them as if he scorned that what he asked for lay in their power to give.
BRUTUS. Come, we'll tell them what we've done here. I know they're waiting for us in the marketplace.
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 3 — Rome. The Forum
paragraphs: Enter seven or eight Citizens.
FIRST CITIZEN. Once and for all, if he asks for our votes, we shouldn't refuse him.
SECOND CITIZEN. We may, sir, if we want to.

THIRD CITIZEN. We have the power to do it ourselves, but it's a power we have no power to use. If he shows us his wounds and tells us his deeds, we're meant to put our tongues into those wounds and speak for them. So if he tells us his noble deeds, we must tell him how nobly we accept them. Ingratitude is monstrous. For the multitude to be ungrateful would make a monster of the multitude, and since we're part of it, we'd make ourselves monstrous parts.
FIRST CITIZEN. And it wouldn't take much to make us thought no better of. Once, when we stood up over the corn, he didn't hesitate to call us the many-headed multitude.

THIRD CITIZEN. We've been called that by many. It's not because our heads are some brown, some black, some auburn, some bald, but because our wits are so differently colored. And truly, I think if all our wits came out of one skull, they'd fly east, west, north and south, and their agreement to go one direct way would be to go all at once to every point of the compass.
SECOND CITIZEN. You think so? Which way do you think my wit would fly?
THIRD CITIZEN. Well, your wit won't get out as quickly as another man's. It's wedged in tight inside a blockhead. But if it were free, it would surely go south.
SECOND CITIZEN. Why that way?
THIRD CITIZEN. To lose itself in a fog. Three parts of it would melt away in the rotten dews, and the fourth would come back out of conscience, to help get you a wife.
SECOND CITIZEN. You're never without your tricks. Go on, go on.
THIRD CITIZEN. Are you all resolved to give your votes? But that doesn't matter. The greater number carries it. I say, if he would lean toward the people, there was never a worthier man.
Enter Coriolanus in a gown of humility, with Menenius.

Here he comes, in the gown of humility. Watch his behavior. We're not to stay all together, but to pass him where he stands, by ones, by twos and by threes. He's to make his requests to each of us separately, so every one of us has the single honor of giving him our own vote with our own tongue. So follow me, and I'll tell you how to go past him.
ALL. Agreed, agreed.
[_Exeunt._]
MENENIUS. Oh sir, you're not doing this right. Haven't you known that the worthiest men have done it?

CORIOLANUS. What must I say? "Please, sir," a plague on it! I can't make my tongue go at that pace. "Look, sir, my wounds! I got them in my country's service, when some of your brothers roared and ran from the noise of our own drums."
MENENIUS. Oh, by the gods! You must not speak of that. You must ask them to think well of you.
CORIOLANUS. Think well of me! Hang them! I wish they'd forget me, the way they forget the virtues our priests preach to them.
MENENIUS. You'll ruin everything. I'll leave you. Please speak to them, I beg you, in a wholesome manner.
[_Exit Menenius._]
CORIOLANUS. Tell them to wash their faces and keep their teeth clean.
Enter three of the Citizens.
So, here comes a pair. You know the reason, sirs, why I'm standing here.
THIRD CITIZEN. We do, sir. Tell us what brought you to it.
CORIOLANUS. My own merit.
SECOND CITIZEN. Your own merit?
CORIOLANUS. Yes, but not my own desire.
THIRD CITIZEN. What, not your own desire?
CORIOLANUS. No, sir. It was never my desire to trouble the poor with begging.
THIRD CITIZEN. You must think that if we give you anything, we hope to gain by you.
CORIOLANUS. Well then, please, what's the price of the consulship?
FIRST CITIZEN. The price is to ask for it kindly.
CORIOLANUS. Kindly, sir, please, let me have it. I have wounds to show you, which you can see in private. Your good vote, sir. What do you say?
SECOND CITIZEN. You shall have it, worthy sir.
CORIOLANUS. It's a deal, sir. That's two worthy votes begged in all. I have your alms. Goodbye.
THIRD CITIZEN. But this is somewhat odd.
SECOND CITIZEN. If it were to give again, but it doesn't matter.
[_Exeunt two citizens._]
Enter two other Citizens.
CORIOLANUS. Please now, if it fits the tune of your votes that I may be consul, I have the customary gown here.
FOURTH CITIZEN. You have deserved nobly of your country, and you have not deserved nobly.
CORIOLANUS. Your riddle?
FOURTH CITIZEN. You have been a scourge to her enemies, and you have been a rod to her friends. You have not really loved the common people.

CORIOLANUS. You should think me the more virtuous because I haven't been common in my love. Sir, I will flatter my sworn brother the people, to earn a dearer opinion of them. They count that a gentle quality. And since the wisdom of their choice is to want my hat rather than my heart, I'll practice the winning nod and bow to them with the best fakery. That is, sir, I will fake the charm of some popular man and give it generously to those who want it. So I beg you, let me be consul.
FIFTH CITIZEN. We hope to find you our friend, and so we give you our votes heartily.
FOURTH CITIZEN. You have received many wounds for your country.
CORIOLANUS. I won't seal your knowledge of that by showing them. I'll make much of your votes, and so trouble you no further.
BOTH CITIZENS. The gods give you joy, sir, heartily.
[_Exeunt citizens._]

CORIOLANUS. Most sweet voices! Better to die, better to starve, than beg for the pay we have already earned. Why should I stand here in this wolfish gown, begging Hob and Dick for their needless votes? Custom calls me to it. But if we must do whatever custom wants, in all things, then the dust on ancient time would lie unswept, and the mountain of error would be piled too high for truth to see over. Rather than play the fool like this, let the high office and the honor go to someone who would do this. I'm halfway through. I've endured one part, and I'll do the other.
Enter three Citizens more.

Here come more voices. Your votes! For your votes I have fought. For your votes I have kept watch. For your votes I carry more than two dozen wounds. I have seen and heard of eighteen battles. For your votes I have done many things, some less, some more. Your votes! Indeed, I would be consul.
SIXTH CITIZEN. He has done nobly, and he can't go without any honest man's vote.
SEVENTH CITIZEN. So let him be consul. May the gods give him joy and make him a good friend to the people!
ALL THREE CITIZENS. Amen, amen. God save you, noble consul.
[_Exeunt citizens._]
CORIOLANUS. Worthy voices!
Enter Menenius with Brutus and Sicinius.
MENENIUS. You have served out your required time, and the tribunes give you the people's vote. What remains is that, dressed in the marks of office, you meet the Senate soon.
CORIOLANUS. Is this done?
SICINIUS. You have completed the custom of asking. The people accept you, and they are summoned to meet soon to confirm your appointment.
CORIOLANUS. Where? At the Senate House?
SICINIUS. There, Coriolanus.
CORIOLANUS. May I change these clothes?
SICINIUS. You may, sir.
CORIOLANUS. I'll do that right away and, being myself again, go to the Senate House.
MENENIUS. I'll keep you company. Will you come along?
BRUTUS. We're staying here for the people.
SICINIUS. Goodbye.
[_Exeunt Coriolanus and Menenius._]
He has it now, and from his looks, I think it's warm at his heart.
BRUTUS. He wore his humble clothes with a proud heart. Will you dismiss the people?
Enter the Pebleians.
SICINIUS. Well, my masters, have you chosen this man?
FIRST CITIZEN. He has our votes, sir.
BRUTUS. We pray the gods he may deserve your love.
SECOND CITIZEN. Amen, sir. To my poor, unworthy notice, he mocked us when he begged our votes.
THIRD CITIZEN. Certainly, he flat-out insulted us.
FIRST CITIZEN. No, that's just his way of speaking. He didn't mock us.
SECOND CITIZEN. Not one of us, except you, but says he treated us with scorn. He should have shown us his marks of merit, the wounds he received for his country.
SICINIUS. Why, so he did, I'm sure.
ALL. No, no. No one saw them.

THIRD CITIZEN. He said he had wounds that he could show in private. Then he waved his hat, like this, in scorn, and said, "I would be consul. Aged custom won't allow it except by your votes. Your votes, then." When we granted that, here came, "I thank you for your votes. Thank you. Your most sweet votes! Now that you've given up your votes, I have nothing more to do with you." Wasn't this mockery?
SICINIUS. Why, were you either too ignorant to see it, or, seeing it, so childishly friendly as to give your votes anyway?

BRUTUS. Couldn't you have told him what you were taught to say? When he had no power and was a petty servant of the state, he was your enemy. He always spoke against your liberties and the charters you hold as part of the commonwealth. And now that he's reaching a place of power and sway in the state, if he should remain a bitter, fixed enemy of the plebeians, your votes might be curses on yourselves. You should have said that since his worthy deeds claimed no less than what he stood for, his gracious nature would think of you for your votes. It would turn his malice toward you into love, and he would stand as your friendly lord.

SICINIUS. To have said this, as you were advised beforehand, would have touched his spirit and tested his inclination. It would have drawn out of him either a gracious promise, which you could have held him to as the occasion called for, or else it would have galled his surly nature, which can't easily bear terms tying him to anything. That would have put him in a rage, and you should have taken advantage of his anger and passed him over unelected.

BRUTUS. Did you notice that he asked for your votes in open contempt when he needed your love? Do you think his contempt won't bruise you when he has the power to crush? Why, did none of you have a heart in your bodies? Or did you have tongues only to shout against the guidance of good judgment?
SICINIUS. Have you ever before refused someone who asked, and now give your much-begged tongues to a man who didn't ask but mocked?
THIRD CITIZEN. He's not confirmed yet. We can still refuse him.
SECOND CITIZEN. And we will refuse him. I'll get five hundred votes to say so.
FIRST CITIZEN. I'll get twice five hundred, and their friends to make up the number.

BRUTUS. Get out of here at once and tell those friends they have chosen a consul who will take their liberties from them. He'll make them no more heard than dogs that are beaten as often for barking as they're kept for it.

SICINIUS. Let them assemble and, on safer judgment, all revoke your ignorant election. Stress his pride and his old hatred of you. Also, don't forget with what contempt he wore the humble gown, and how he scorned you in his request. But your love, thinking of his services, took from you any grasp of how he was acting then. He did it most mockingly and without dignity, shaped by the old hatred he bears you.
BRUTUS. Put the blame on us, your tribunes. Say that we worked at it, with no obstacle in between, so that you had to cast your choice on him.

SICINIUS. Say you chose him more at our command than guided by your own true feelings. Say your minds were taken up with what you felt you had to do rather than what you should, and that made you vote him consul against the grain. Put the blame on us.

BRUTUS. Yes, don't spare us. Say we lectured you on how young he began to serve his country, how long he has kept at it, and what stock he comes from. It's the noble house of the Martians, from which came Ancus Martius, Numa's daughter's son, who was king after the great Hostilius. Publius and Quintus, who brought our best water here by channels, were of the same house. And Censorinus, who was so named, and nobly named so, for being censor twice, was his great ancestor.

SICINIUS. One descended like this, who has also done well himself to deserve a high place, we recommended to your memory. But you've found, weighing his present behavior against his past, that he's your fixed enemy, and you revoke your sudden approval.
BRUTUS. Say you'd never have done it, and keep hammering on that, except that we pushed you. And right away, when you've gathered your numbers, go to the Capitol.
ALL. We will. Almost all of us regret our choice.
[_Exeunt Plebeians._]

BRUTUS. Let them go. It's better to risk this mutiny now than to wait, with no doubt of a greater one. If, as is his nature, he flies into a rage at their refusal, both watch for and answer the advantage of his anger.
SICINIUS. To the Capitol, come. We'll be there ahead of the stream of the people. This will seem, as it partly is, their own doing, though we have goaded them on.
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 1 — Rome. A street
paragraphs: Cornets. Enter Coriolanus, Menenius, all the Gentry, Cominius, Titus Lartius and other Senators.
CORIOLANUS. So Tullus Aufidius had raised a new army?
LARTIUS. He had, my lord, and that is what made them agree to terms so quickly.
CORIOLANUS. So the Volsces are in the same position as at first. They're ready to attack us again whenever the time prompts them.
COMINIUS. They are so worn down, lord consul, that we will hardly live to see their banners raised again.
CORIOLANUS. Did you see Aufidius?
LARTIUS. He came to me under a safe-conduct and cursed the Volsces for giving up the town so shamefully. He has retired to Antium.
CORIOLANUS. Did he speak of me?
LARTIUS. He did, my lord.
CORIOLANUS. How? What did he say?

LARTIUS. He spoke of how often he had met you sword to sword. He said that of everything on earth he hates you most. He said he would stake his whole fortune, with no hope of getting it back, if only he could be called your conqueror.
CORIOLANUS. He lives at Antium?
LARTIUS. At Antium.
CORIOLANUS. I wish I had a reason to go and find him there, so I could face his hatred head on. Welcome home.
Enter Sicinius and Brutus.
Look, here are the tribunes of the people, the tongues of the common mouth. I despise them. They dress themselves up in authority in a way no noble should have to put up with.
SICINIUS. Go no further.
CORIOLANUS. Ha? What's this?
BRUTUS. It will be dangerous to go on. No further.
CORIOLANUS. What causes this change?
MENENIUS. What's the matter?
COMINIUS. Hasn't he been approved by both the nobles and the commoners?
BRUTUS. No, Cominius.
CORIOLANUS. Did I get votes from children?
FIRST SENATOR. Tribunes, give way. He must go to the marketplace.
BRUTUS. The people are furious with him.
SICINIUS. Stop, or everything will break out in a brawl.

CORIOLANUS. Are these your herd? Must these people have votes, when they can give them now and then at once take back their word? What is your job? You are their mouths, so why don't you control their teeth? Haven't you set them on?
MENENIUS. Be calm, be calm.
CORIOLANUS. This is deliberate. It grows out of a plot to curb the will of the nobility. Put up with it, and you will live with people who can't rule and never will accept being ruled.

BRUTUS. Don't call it a plot. The people cry that you mocked them. And recently, when grain was given to them free, you objected. You slandered those who spoke up for the people, calling them time-servers, flatterers and enemies of the nobility.
CORIOLANUS. Why, this was known before.
BRUTUS. Not to all of them.
CORIOLANUS. Have you told them since?
BRUTUS. What? Me, tell them?
COMINIUS. You're the sort to do that kind of business.
BRUTUS. Not unlikely, either way, to do it better than you.
CORIOLANUS. Then why should I be consul? By those clouds, let me deserve as badly as you do, and make me your fellow tribune.

SICINIUS. You show too much of the very thing that stirs the people up. If you want to reach where you're headed, you must ask the way, since you've lost it, in a gentler spirit. Otherwise you will never be as noble as a consul, or be yoked with him as tribune.
MENENIUS. Let's be calm.
COMINIUS. The people are being deceived and egged on. This trickery doesn't suit Rome. And Coriolanus doesn't deserve this shameful obstruction, falsely thrown in the plain road of his merit.
CORIOLANUS. Tell me about the grain? This was my speech, and I will say it again.
MENENIUS. Not now, not now.
FIRST SENATOR. Not in this heat, sir, not now.

CORIOLANUS. Now, as I live, I will. My nobler friends, I beg their pardon. As for the fickle, foul-smelling many, let them look at me, since I don't flatter, and see themselves in it. I say again, by humoring them we feed the weed of rebellion, insolence and sedition against our Senate. We ourselves ploughed for it, sowed it and scattered it, by mixing them in with us, the honored few. We lack neither virtue nor power. We lack only what we have given to beggars.
MENENIUS. Well, no more.
FIRST SENATOR. No more words, we beg you.

CORIOLANUS. What? No more? I have shed my blood for my country, not fearing any outside force. In the same way my lungs will coin words until they wear out, against those measles. We scorn the thought of being covered in their blotches, yet we went looking for the very way to catch them.
BRUTUS. You speak of the people as if you were a god who punishes, and not a man with their weaknesses.
SICINIUS. It would be good to let the people know it.
MENENIUS. What, what? It's only his temper.
CORIOLANUS. Temper? If I were as calm as sleep at midnight, by Jove, this would still be my mind.
SICINIUS. It is a mind that will stay a poison where it is, and will not poison anyone further.
CORIOLANUS. "Will stay"? Do you hear this Triton of the minnows, the sea-god lording it over tiny fish? Do you hear his absolute "shall"?
COMINIUS. It came from the law.

CORIOLANUS. "Shall"? Oh, good but most unwise patricians! You grave but reckless senators, have you let the Hydra, the many-headed monster, choose an officer for itself? He is only the horn and the noise of the monster, yet with his commanding "shall" he has the nerve to say he'll turn your river into a ditch and make your channel his own. If he has power, then lower your heads in shame at your ignorance. If he has none, wake up from your dangerous softness. If you are wise, don't act like common fools. If you are not, let them have cushions beside you. You are plebeians if they are senators. And they are no less than that when your votes and theirs are blended, and the strongest flavor is theirs. They choose their magistrate, and he is the kind of man who sets his "shall," his popular "shall," against a more serious bench than ever frowned in Greece. By Jove himself, it makes the consuls look base! And my soul aches to think how soon, when two authorities are up and neither is supreme, confusion may enter the gap between them and make one swallow the other.
COMINIUS. Well, on to the marketplace.
CORIOLANUS. Whoever gave the advice to hand out the grain from the storehouse free, as was done at times in Greece—
MENENIUS. Well, well, no more of that.
CORIOLANUS. Though the people there had more absolute power, I say they fed disobedience and fed the ruin of the state.
BRUTUS. Why should the people give their votes to a man who talks like this?
