CORIOLANUS. I'll give my reasons, worthier ones than their votes. They know the grain was not a reward, for they were well aware they never did any service to earn it. They were called up for the war, but even when the very heart of the state was in danger, they would not go through the gates. That kind of service did not deserve free grain. Once in the war, their mutinies and revolts, in which they showed the most courage, did not speak for them either. The accusation they have often made against the Senate could never have come from our generous gift, since no such cause had yet arisen. Well, what then? How will this crowd, with their hearts so close to the surface, digest the Senate's kindness? Let their deeds show what their words will probably be: "We asked for it. We are the larger number, and in real fear they gave us what we demanded." That is how we lower the nature of our seats, and make the rabble call our care for them fear. In time this will break open the locks of the Senate and let in the crows to peck at the eagles.
MENENIUS. Come, enough.
BRUTUS. Enough, and more than enough.

CORIOLANUS. No, take more! Let everything that can be sworn by, divine and human, seal what I end with. This double rule has one party that rightly despises the other, and another that insults without any reason. Rank, title and wisdom cannot decide anything except by the yes and no of general ignorance. Such a state must neglect real needs and give way to flimsy, unstable whims. With its purpose blocked like this, it follows that nothing is done to any purpose. Therefore, I beg you, you who would rather be wise than fearful, who love the foundation of the state more than you fear changing it, who prefer a noble life to a long one, and who are willing to risk a dangerous medicine on a body that is sure to die without it: pluck out the many-tongued crowd's tongue at once. Don't let them lick the sweet thing that is their poison. Your dishonor mangles true judgment and robs the state of the soundness it should have. It no longer has the power to do the good it wants to do, because of the evil that controls it.
BRUTUS. He has said enough.
SICINIUS. He has spoken like a traitor, and will answer as traitors do.

CORIOLANUS. You wretch, may contempt overwhelm you! What should the people do with these bald tribunes? Their obedience depends on them, and so it fails toward the greater bench, the Senate. These tribunes were chosen during a rebellion, when what must be done, not what was proper, was law. In a better hour, let what is proper be declared necessary, and throw their power in the dust.
BRUTUS. Plain treason.
SICINIUS. This a consul? No.
BRUTUS. The aediles, ho! Let him be arrested.
Enter an Aedile.
SICINIUS. Go and call the people;
[_Exit Aedile._]
in whose name I myself arrest you as a traitorous innovator and an enemy of the public good. I order you to obey and follow me to answer for it.
CORIOLANUS. Away, old goat.
ALL PATRICIANS. We'll stand surety for him.
COMINIUS.
[_to Sicinius_.] Old sir, hands off.
CORIOLANUS.
[_to Sicinius_.] Away, rotten thing, or I'll shake your bones
out of your clothes.
SICINIUS. Help, citizens!
Enter a rabble of Plebeians with the Aediles.
MENENIUS. More respect on both sides!
SICINIUS. Here's the man who would take all your power from you.
BRUTUS. Seize him, aediles.
ALL PLEBEIANS. Down with him, down with him!
SECOND SENATOR. Weapons, weapons, weapons!
[_They all bustle about Coriolanus._]
Tribunes, patricians, citizens, what, ho! Sicinius, Brutus, Coriolanus, citizens!
ALL. Peace, peace, peace! Stop, hold, peace!
MENENIUS. What is about to happen? I'm out of breath. Chaos is near. I can't speak. You tribunes, to the people! Coriolanus, patience! Speak, good Sicinius.
SICINIUS. Hear me, people! Peace!
ALL PLEBEIANS. Let's hear our tribune. Peace! Speak, speak, speak.
SICINIUS. You are about to lose your liberties. Martius would take everything from you, Martius, whom you recently named for consul.
MENENIUS. Shame, shame, shame! This is the way to kindle a fire, not to put it out.
FIRST SENATOR. This is the way to tear the city down and lay it all flat.
SICINIUS. What is the city but the people?
ALL PLEBEIANS. True, the people are the city.
BRUTUS. By the consent of all, we were established as the people's magistrates.
ALL PLEBEIANS. You remain so.
MENENIUS. And so you are likely to remain.
COMINIUS. That is the way to lay the city flat, to bring the roof down to the foundation, and bury everything that still stands in its own order under heaps and piles of ruin.
SICINIUS. This deserves death.
BRUTUS. Either we stand by our authority or we lose it. On behalf of the people, by whose power we were elected theirs, we here declare that Martius deserves immediate death.
SICINIUS. So lay hold of him, take him to the Tarpeian rock, and throw him from there to his destruction.
BRUTUS. Aediles, seize him!
ALL PLEBEIANS. Yield, Martius, yield!
MENENIUS. Hear me one word. I beg you, tribunes, hear me just one word.
AEDILES. Peace, peace!
MENENIUS. Be what you seem, truly your country's friends, and go calmly about what you want to put right so violently.
BRUTUS. Sir, those cold ways that look like sensible remedies are poison when the disease is violent. Lay hands on him, and take him to the rock.
[_Coriolanus draws his sword._]
CORIOLANUS. No, I'll die here. Some of you have seen me fight. Come, test on yourselves what you have seen me do.
MENENIUS. Down with that sword! Tribunes, withdraw for a while.
BRUTUS. Lay hands on him!
MENENIUS. Help Martius, help! All you who are noble, help him, young and old!
ALL PLEBEIANS. Down with him, down with him!
[_In this mutiny the Tribunes, the Aediles and the People are beat in._]
MENENIUS. Go, get yourself home. Be gone, away. Otherwise everything will be ruined.
SECOND SENATOR. Get away.
CORIOLANUS. Stand firm! We have as many friends as enemies.
MENENIUS. Will it come to that?
FIRST SENATOR. The gods forbid! Please, noble friend, go home. Leave us to cure this matter.
MENENIUS. For it's a sore on us that you can't dress yourself. Be gone, I beg you.
COMINIUS. Come, sir, come along with us.

CORIOLANUS. I wish they were barbarians, as they are, though they were born in Rome like a litter of animals. I wish they were not Romans, as they are not, though they were calved in the porch of the Capitol.
MENENIUS. Be gone! Don't put your worthy rage into your tongue. One time will pay for another.
CORIOLANUS. On fair ground I could beat forty of them.
MENENIUS. I could take on a pair of the best of them myself, yes, even the two tribunes.

COMINIUS. But now the odds are beyond counting, and courage is called foolishness when it stands against a falling building. Will you leave before the rabble returns? Their rage tears like a river that has been blocked, and sweeps away what it is used to carrying.
MENENIUS. Please, be gone. I'll try whether my old wit is wanted by those who have little of their own. This must be patched with cloth of any color.
COMINIUS. No, come away.
[_Exeunt Coriolanus and Cominius._]
PATRICIAN. This man has ruined his fortunes.

MENENIUS. His nature is too noble for the world. He would not flatter Neptune to get his trident, or Jove to get his power to thunder. His heart is his mouth. What his chest forges, his tongue must pour out. And when he's angry, he forgets he ever heard the word death.
[_A noise within._]
Here's fine work.
PATRICIAN. I wish they were in bed!
MENENIUS. I wish they were in the Tiber! What the devil, couldn't he speak to them politely?
Enter Brutus and Sicinius with the rabble again.
SICINIUS. Where is this viper, who would empty the city of people and make every man his own master?
MENENIUS. You worthy tribunes—

SICINIUS. He shall be thrown down the Tarpeian rock by rough hands. He has defied the law, and so the law will give him no further trial than the severity of the public power, which he treats as nothing.
FIRST CITIZEN. He will know well that the noble tribunes are the people's mouths, and we are their hands.
ALL PLEBEIANS. He will, for sure.
MENENIUS. Sir, sir—
SICINIUS. Peace!
MENENIUS. Don't cry havoc, the signal for slaughter, when you should only be hunting within modest limits.
SICINIUS. Sir, how is it that you helped make this rescue?
MENENIUS. Hear me speak. Because I know the consul's worth, I can also name his faults.
SICINIUS. Consul? What consul?
MENENIUS. The consul Coriolanus.
BRUTUS. He, consul?
ALL PLEBEIANS. No, no, no, no, no!
MENENIUS. If, with the tribunes' permission and yours, good people, I may be heard, I would ask for a word or two. They will do you no more harm than the loss of a little time.

SICINIUS. Then speak briefly, for we are determined to dispatch this viper of a traitor. To throw him out of here would be one danger, and to keep him here would be our certain death. Therefore it is decreed that he dies tonight.
MENENIUS. Now the good gods forbid that our renowned Rome, whose gratitude toward her deserving children is written in Jove's own book, should like an unnatural mother now eat up her own.
SICINIUS. He's a disease that must be cut away.

MENENIUS. Oh, he's a limb that has only a disease. Cutting it off would be deadly, but curing it is easy. What has he done to Rome that deserves death? He killed our enemies. The blood he has lost, and I dare swear it is many an ounce more than what he has left, he spilled for his country. And to have what is left lost at his own country's hands would be, for all of us who do it and allow it, a brand of shame until the end of the world.
SICINIUS. This is all crooked talk.
BRUTUS. Completely wrong. When he loved his country, it honored him.
MENENIUS. Once a foot has gone gangrenous, it is not valued for what it was before.
BRUTUS. We'll hear no more. Go after him to his house and drag him out of there, in case his infection, which is catching, spreads further.

MENENIUS. One word more, one word! This tiger-footed rage, when it finds the harm of unconsidered haste, will too late tie lead weights to its heels. Proceed by proper process, in case factions break out, since he is beloved, and sack great Rome with Romans.
BRUTUS. If it were so—
SICINIUS. What are you saying? Haven't we had a taste of his obedience? Our aediles struck! Ourselves resisted! Come.

MENENIUS. Consider this. He has been raised in the wars since he could draw a sword, and is badly schooled in refined speech. He throws out meal and bran together without telling them apart. Give me leave, and I'll go to him and promise to bring him to answer in lawful form, in peace, at his utmost peril.
FIRST SENATOR. Noble tribunes, this is the humane way. The other course will prove too bloody, and its end will be unknown at its beginning.
SICINIUS. Noble Menenius, then act as the people's officer. Masters, lay down your weapons.
BRUTUS. Don't go home.
SICINIUS. Meet in the marketplace. We'll wait for you there. If you don't bring Martius, we'll proceed in our first way.
MENENIUS. I'll bring him to you.
[_To Senators_.] Let me ask for your company. He must come,
or the worst will follow.
FIRST SENATOR. Please, let's go to him.
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 2 — Rome. A room in Coriolanus’s house
paragraphs: Enter Coriolanus with Nobles.

CORIOLANUS. Let them pull everything down around my ears. Let them give me death on the wheel or at the heels of wild horses, or pile ten hills on the Tarpeian rock so that the fall would stretch down beyond the range of sight. I will still be like this toward them.
FIRST PATRICIAN. You do the nobler thing.

CORIOLANUS. I wonder that my mother doesn't approve of me more. She used to call them woollen slaves, things made to buy and sell for pennies, to stand bare-headed in crowds, to yawn, keep still and gape in wonder whenever one man of my rank stood up to speak of peace or war.
Enter Volumnia.
I'm talking about you. Why did you wish me milder? Would you have me false to my nature? Say instead that I play the man I am.
VOLUMNIA. Oh, sir, sir, sir, I would have had you put your power to good use before you had worn it out.
CORIOLANUS. Let it go.

VOLUMNIA. You could have been just as much the man you are by striving less to be so. The thwarting of your wishes would have been less if you had not shown them what you were like before they lacked the power to cross you.
CORIOLANUS. Let them hang!
VOLUMNIA. Yes, and burn too.
Enter Menenius with the Senators.
MENENIUS. Come, come, you have been too rough, rather too rough. You must go back and mend it.
FIRST SENATOR. There's no other remedy, unless our good city is to split down the middle and perish by our not doing it.
VOLUMNIA. Please be advised. I have a heart as unwilling to bend as yours, but a brain that leads me to use my anger to better advantage.

MENENIUS. Well said, noble woman. Before he should stoop like this to the herd, I would put on my armor, which I can scarcely bear. But the violent fit of the times demands it as medicine for the whole state.
CORIOLANUS. What must I do?
MENENIUS. Go back to the tribunes.
CORIOLANUS. Well, and then? And then?
MENENIUS. Take back what you have said.
CORIOLANUS. For them? I couldn't do it for the gods. Must I then do it for them?

VOLUMNIA. You are too uncompromising, though you can never be too noble in that, except when extremes are speaking. I have heard you say that honor and policy, like inseparable friends, grow together in war. Grant that, and tell me what each of them loses by the other in peace, so that they don't join together there.
CORIOLANUS. Tush, tush!
MENENIUS. A good question.

VOLUMNIA. If it is honorable in your wars to seem what you are not, which you do through your policy for your best ends, how is it any less honorable or worse for policy to keep company with honor in peace as in war, since both of them need it equally?
CORIOLANUS. Why do you press this?

VOLUMNIA. Because now you must speak to the people, not by your own instruction, nor with what your heart prompts, but with words that are rooted only in your tongue. They are bastards and mere syllables, with no approval from the truth in your heart. Now, this dishonors you no more than taking a town with gentle words would, when otherwise you would have to try your luck and risk much bloodshed. If my fortunes and my friends were at stake, and honor allowed it, I would pretend against my own nature. In this I speak for your wife, your son, these senators and the nobles. And you would rather show our common louts how well you can frown than spend one fawning word on them to win the inheritance of their love and to protect what the lack of it might ruin.
MENENIUS. Noble lady! Come, go with us and speak fair. By doing so you may heal not just the danger of the present, but the loss of what is past.

VOLUMNIA. Please now, my son, go to them with this cap in your hand. Hold it out as far as this, and here stand before them, with your knee kissing the stones. In such business action is eloquence, and the eyes of the ignorant are more learned than their ears. Wave your head, which often corrects your stout heart this way, and be humble now, like the ripest mulberry that won't bear handling. Or say to them that you are their soldier, bred in battles, and you lack the soft manner that you admit would suit you to use, as they have a right to claim it, when asking for their good love. But say that from now on you will, in truth, make yourself theirs, as far as you have power and person.
MENENIUS. Just do this exactly as she says, and their hearts would be yours. For when they are asked, they give pardons as freely as words to little purpose.
VOLUMNIA. Please now, go, and be ruled. Though I know you would rather follow your enemy into a fiery pit than flatter him in a lady's chamber.
Enter Cominius.
Here is Cominius.
COMINIUS. I have been in the marketplace. Sir, it is right that you either gather a strong party or defend yourself by calmness or by staying away. Everything there is in anger.
MENENIUS. Only fair speech will do.
COMINIUS. I think it will serve, if he can shape his spirit to it.
VOLUMNIA. He must, and he will. Please now, say you will, and go about it.

CORIOLANUS. Must I go show them my bare, unprotected head? Must I with my base tongue give my noble heart a lie that it must bear? Well, I will do it. Yet if there were only this one plot of ground to lose, this mold of Martius, they could grind it to dust and throw it against the wind. To the marketplace! You have put me in such a part that I will never play it true to life.
COMINIUS. Come, come, we'll prompt you.
VOLUMNIA. Please now, sweet son. As you have said, my praises made you a soldier first. So, to earn my praise for this, perform a part you have never played before.

CORIOLANUS. Well, I must do it. Away, my nature, and possess me with some harlot's spirit! Let my throat of war, which sang in chorus with my drum, be turned into a pipe as small as a eunuch's or the girlish voice that lulls babies to sleep! Let the smiles of knaves lodge in my cheeks, and schoolboys' tears fill the lenses of my eyes! Let a beggar's tongue move through my lips, and let my armored knees, which bowed only in my stirrup, bend like those of a man who has received a handout! I will not do it, in case I cease to honor my own truth and, by the action of my body, teach my mind a deep-rooted baseness.

VOLUMNIA. Then it is your choice. To beg of you is more dishonor to me than your begging of them is to you. Let everything go to ruin. Let your mother feel your pride rather than fear your dangerous stubbornness, for I mock at death with as big a heart as you. Do as you please. Your bravery was mine. You sucked it from me. But you owe your pride to yourself.

CORIOLANUS. Please, be content. Mother, I am going to the marketplace. Scold me no more. I'll play the quack and sell them my charm, cheat their hearts out of them, and come home loved by every trade in Rome. Look, I am going. Give my regards to my wife. I'll return consul, or never trust what my tongue can do in the way of flattery again.
VOLUMNIA. Do as you will.
[_Exit Volumnia._]
COMINIUS. Away! The tribunes are waiting for you. Arm yourself to answer mildly, for they are prepared, as I hear, with accusations stronger than any yet brought against you.
CORIOLANUS. The word is "mildly." Please, let's go. Let them accuse me with inventions. I will answer in my honor.
MENENIUS. Yes, but mildly.
CORIOLANUS. Well, mildly it shall be, then. Mildly.
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 3 — Rome. The Forum
paragraphs: Enter Sicinius and Brutus.

BRUTUS. On this point charge him hard: that he wants tyrannical power. If he slips away from us there, press him with his hatred of the people, and with the fact that the plunder taken from the Antiates was never shared out.
Enter an Aedile.
What, will he come?
AEDILE. He's coming.
BRUTUS. Who is with him?
AEDILE. Old Menenius, and those senators who have always favored him.
SICINIUS. Do you have a list of all the votes we have secured, set down head by head?
AEDILE. I have. It's ready.
SICINIUS. Have you gathered them by tribes?
AEDILE. I have.

SICINIUS. Assemble the people here at once. When they hear me say "It shall be so, by the right and strength of the commons," whether it is for death, a fine or banishment, then let them cry out. If I say "Fine," let them cry "Fine." If "Death," let them cry "Death." They should insist on their old privilege and power, in the justice of the cause.
AEDILE. I'll tell them.
BRUTUS. And once they have begun to cry out, let them not stop. With a confused din, let them demand the immediate carrying out of whatever sentence we happen to pass.
AEDILE. Very well.
SICINIUS. Make them strong and ready for this signal when we happen to give it.
BRUTUS. Go about it.
[_Exit Aedile._]

Make him angry at once. He has always been used to winning and to getting his fill of contradiction. Once he's provoked, he can't be reined in to calm again. Then he says what is in his heart, and that is what will help us break his neck.
Enter Coriolanus, Menenius and Cominius with other Senators.
SICINIUS. Well, here he comes.
MENENIUS. Calmly, I beg you.

CORIOLANUS. Yes, calm as a stable-hand who, for the smallest coin, will take being called a knave by the volume. May the honored gods keep Rome safe and the seats of justice filled with worthy men! Plant love among us! Fill our wide temples with shows of peace, and not our streets with war!
FIRST SENATOR. Amen, amen.
MENENIUS. A noble wish.
Enter the Aedile with the Plebeians.
SICINIUS. Come near, you people.
AEDILE. Listen to your tribunes. Attention! Peace, I say!
CORIOLANUS. First, hear me speak.
BOTH TRIBUNES. Well, say it. Peace, ho!
CORIOLANUS. Will I be charged with nothing further than what is before us now? Must everything be decided here?
SICINIUS. I demand to know whether you submit to the people's votes, accept their officers, and are content to suffer lawful punishment for whatever faults are proved against you.
CORIOLANUS. I am content.
MENENIUS. Look, citizens, he says he is content. Consider the war service he has done. Think of the wounds his body bears, which look like graves in the holy churchyard.
CORIOLANUS. Scratches from briars, scars that only move people to laughter.

MENENIUS. Consider further that when he doesn't speak like a citizen, you find him speaking like a soldier. Don't take his rougher tone for malicious sounds. Take it, as I say, as the manner of a soldier rather than of someone who hates you.
COMINIUS. Well, well, no more.
CORIOLANUS. What is the matter, that after being approved for consul by full vote, I am so dishonored that in the very hour you take it away again?
SICINIUS. Answer to us.
CORIOLANUS. Say it, then. It's true, I ought to.
SICINIUS. We charge you with plotting to take from Rome all her seasoned offices and to wind your way into tyrannical power. For this you are a traitor to the people.
CORIOLANUS. What? Traitor?
MENENIUS. No, calmly! Your promise.

CORIOLANUS. May the fires in the lowest hell wrap around the people! Call me their traitor? You injurious tribune! Even if twenty thousand deaths sat in your eyes, as many millions were clutched in your hands, and both numbers were in your lying tongue, I would say "You lie" to you in a voice as free as the one I use to pray to the gods.
SICINIUS. Do you mark this, people?
ALL PLEBEIANS. To the rock, to the rock with him!

SICINIUS. Peace! We need not add any new matter to his charge. You have seen what he did and heard what he said: beating your officers, cursing you yourselves, opposing the laws with blows, and here defying those whose great power must try him. Even this, so criminal and of such a capital kind, deserves the extreme penalty of death.
BRUTUS. But since he has served Rome well—
CORIOLANUS. What are you chattering about service?
BRUTUS. I'm talking about what I know.
CORIOLANUS. You?
MENENIUS. Is this the promise you made your mother?
COMINIUS. Know, I beg you—

CORIOLANUS. I'll know no more. Let them pronounce the steep Tarpeian death, vagabond exile, flaying, or being shut up to linger on a single grain a day. I would not buy their mercy at the price of one fair word. Nor would I hold back my courage because of what they can give, just to have it by saying "Good morning."

SICINIUS. Because he has, as far as he is able, from time to time hated the people, looking for ways to pluck away their power, and as now at last has struck hostile blows, not in the presence of dreaded justice but on the ministers who dispense it, in the name of the people and in the power of us the tribunes, we banish him from our city from this instant. If he returns, he risks being thrown from the Tarpeian rock, and he may never again enter our gates of Rome. In the people's name, I say it shall be so.
ALL PLEBEIANS. It shall be so, it shall be so! Let him go! He's banished, and it shall be so.
COMINIUS. Hear me, my masters and my common friends—
SICINIUS. He's sentenced. No more hearing.

COMINIUS. Let me speak. I have been consul, and I can show on my body the marks of Rome's enemies. I love my country's good with a respect more tender, more holy and more profound than my own life, my dear wife's esteem, the offspring of her womb, and the treasure of my loins. Then if I were to say that—
SICINIUS. We know your drift. Say what?
BRUTUS. There's no more to be said, except that he is banished as an enemy to the people and his country. It shall be so.
ALL PLEBEIANS. It shall be so, it shall be so!

CORIOLANUS. You common cry of curs! I hate your breath like the stink of rotten swamps. I value your love like the dead bodies of unburied men that foul my air. I banish you! Stay here with your uncertainty. Let every feeble rumor shake your hearts. Let your enemies, with the nodding of their helmet plumes, fan you into despair. Keep the power to banish your defenders, until at last your ignorance, which understands nothing until it feels the blow, and which looks only to save yourselves and so is always your own enemy, hands you over as the most abject captives to some nation that conquered you without a fight! Despising the city for your sake, I turn my back like this. There is a world elsewhere.
[_Exeunt Coriolanus, Cominius, with other Senators._]
AEDILE. The people's enemy is gone, is gone.
ALL PLEBEIANS. Our enemy is banished. He is gone. Hoo, hoo!
[_They all shout and throw up their caps._]
SICINIUS. Go see him out the gates, and follow him as he has followed you, with all scorn. Give him the vexation he deserves. Let a guard attend us through the city.
ALL PLEBEIANS. Come, come, let's see him out the gates! Come! The gods preserve our noble tribunes! Come.
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 1 — Rome. Before a gate of the city
paragraphs: Enter Coriolanus, Volumnia, Virgilia, Menenius, Cominius with the young nobility of Rome.

CORIOLANUS. Come, stop your tears. A short farewell. The many-headed beast butts me away. No, mother, where is your old courage? You used to say that extremes are the test of the spirit. You said that ordinary misfortunes can be borne by ordinary men. You said that when the sea is calm, all boats show equal skill at floating. And when fortune's blows strike home hardest, to be wounded and stay gentle takes a noble skill. You used to load me with sayings that would make invincible the heart that learned them.
VIRGILIA. Oh heavens! Oh heavens!
CORIOLANUS. No, please, woman—
VOLUMNIA. Now may the red plague strike every trade in Rome, and may all their occupations perish!

CORIOLANUS. What, what, what! I shall be loved when I am missed. No, mother, take up again that spirit with which you used to say that if you had been the wife of Hercules, you would have done six of his labors and saved your husband that much sweat. Cominius, don't droop. Goodbye. Farewell, my wife, my mother. I'll do well yet. You, old and true Menenius, your tears are saltier than a younger man's and poisonous to your eyes. My former general, I have seen you stern, and you have often looked on hardening sights. Tell these sad women that it is as foolish to wail over unavoidable blows as it is to laugh at them. My mother, you know well that my dangers have always been your comfort. And, do not take this lightly, though I go alone, like a lonely dragon whose swamp makes him feared and talked about more than seen, your son will either rise above the common run or be caught by cunning baits and schemes.
VOLUMNIA. My first son, where will you go? Take good Cominius with you for a while. Decide on some course, more than a wild exposure to every chance that springs up in front of you on the way.
VIRGILIA. Oh the gods!

COMINIUS. I'll follow you for a month and work out with you where you shall settle, so that you may hear of us and we of you. Then if the time brings up a reason for your recall, we won't have to send across the vast world to look for a single man and lose our advantage, which always cools in the absence of the one who needs it.

CORIOLANUS. Fare you well. You are old, and too full of the wars' excesses to go roaming with a man who is not yet bruised. Just bring me out to the gate. Come, my sweet wife, my dearest mother, and my friends of proven nobility. When I am out, say goodbye to me, and smile. Please, come. As long as I remain above the ground, you will hear from me, and you will never hear anything of me except what is like me as I was before.
MENENIUS. That is as worthy as any ear could wish to hear. Come, let's not weep. If I could shake off just seven years from these old arms and legs, by the good gods, I would go with you every step.
CORIOLANUS. Give me your hand. Come.
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 2 — Rome. A street near the gate
paragraphs: Enter two Tribunes, Sicinius, Brutus with the Aedile.
SICINIUS. Tell them all to go home. He's gone, and we'll go no further. The nobility are angry, and we see they have taken his side.
BRUTUS. Now that we have shown our power, let us seem humbler now that it is done than we were while it was being done.
SICINIUS. Tell them to go home. Say their great enemy is gone, and they stand in their ancient strength.
BRUTUS. Send them home.
[_Exit Aedile._]
Here comes his mother.
Enter Volumnia, Virgilia and Menenius.
SICINIUS. Let's not meet her.
BRUTUS. Why?
SICINIUS. They say she's mad.
BRUTUS. They have noticed us. Keep on your way.
VOLUMNIA. Oh, you're well met. May the hoarded plague of the gods repay your love!
MENENIUS. Peace, peace! Don't be so loud.
VOLUMNIA. If I could stop weeping, you would hear. No, and you shall hear some. [_To Sicinius_.] Will you be gone?
VIRGILIA.
[_To Brutus_.] You shall stay too. I wish I had the power
to say so to my husband.
SICINIUS. Are you a man-woman?
VOLUMNIA. Yes, fool, is that a shame? Just note this, fool. Wasn't a man my father? Did you have the cunning of a fox to banish him who struck more blows for Rome than you have spoken words?
SICINIUS. Oh blessed heavens!

VOLUMNIA. More noble blows than you ever spoke wise words, and for Rome's good. I'll tell you what. Yet go. No, you shall stay too. I wish my son were in Arabia, with your tribe before him and his good sword in his hand.
SICINIUS. What then?
VIRGILIA. What then? He would put an end to your descendants.
VOLUMNIA. Bastards and all. Good man, the wounds that he bears for Rome!
MENENIUS. Come, come, peace.
SICINIUS. I wish he had continued toward his country as he began, and not undone the noble bond he made.
BRUTUS. I wish he had.
VOLUMNIA. "I wish he had"? You incensed the rabble. You cats, who can judge his worth as well as I can judge those mysteries which heaven will not let Earth know.
BRUTUS. Please, let's go.

VOLUMNIA. Now, please, sir, get yourself gone. You have done a brave deed. Before you go, hear this. As far as the Capitol exceeds the meanest house in Rome, so far my son, this lady's husband here, this one, do you see, whom you have banished, exceeds you all.
BRUTUS. Well, well, we'll leave you.
SICINIUS. Why do we stay to be baited by a woman who has lost her wits?
[_Exeunt Tribunes._]
VOLUMNIA. Take my prayers with you. I wish the gods had nothing else to do but confirm my curses. If I could meet them just once a day, it would clear my heart of what lies heavy on it.
MENENIUS. You have told them off thoroughly, and, by my word, you have cause. Will you have supper with me?
VOLUMNIA. Anger is my food. I feed on myself and so will starve by eating. Come, let's go. Leave this faint whining, and lament as I do, in anger, like Juno. Come, come, come.
[_Exeunt._]
MENENIUS. Shame, shame, shame!
[_Exit Menenius._]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 3 — A highway between Rome and Antium
paragraphs: Enter a Roman and a Volsce.
ROMAN. I know you well, sir, and you know me. Your name, I think, is Adrian.
VOLSCE. It is, sir. Truly, I've forgotten you.
ROMAN. I am a Roman, but I serve against Rome, just as you do. Do you know me yet?
VOLSCE. Nicanor, isn't it?
ROMAN. The same, sir.
VOLSCE. You had more beard when I last saw you, but your voice proves who you are. What's the news in Rome? I have orders from the Volscian state to find you there. You've saved me a day's journey.
ROMAN. There have been strange uprisings in Rome, the people against the senators, patricians and nobles.
VOLSCE. There have been? Is it over, then? Our state doesn't think so. They're making ready for war, and they hope to attack the Romans while they're still burning with their divisions.

ROMAN. The worst of the blaze is past, but a small thing would make it flare up again. The nobles have taken the banishment of that worthy Coriolanus so much to heart that they're ready to take all power away from the people and strip them of their tribunes for good. This is smoldering, I can tell you, and it's nearly ripe for a violent outbreak.
VOLSCE. Coriolanus banished?
ROMAN. Banished, sir.
VOLSCE. You'll be welcome with this news, Nicanor.

ROMAN. The timing is good for your side now. I've heard it said that the best time to seduce a man's wife is when she's quarreling with her husband. Your noble Tullus Aufidius will shine in these wars, now that his great rival Coriolanus is no longer wanted by his own country.
VOLSCE. He can't fail. I'm very lucky to run into you like this. You've finished my errand, and I'll gladly travel home with you.
ROMAN. Between now and supper I'll tell you most strange things from Rome, all of them good for their enemies. Have you an army ready, you say?
VOLSCE. A magnificent one. The centurions and their companies are separately quartered, already on pay, and ready to march within an hour's warning.
ROMAN. I'm glad to hear they're ready, and I think I'm the man who will set them in motion right now. So, sir, well met, and I'm very glad of your company.
VOLSCE. You take the words out of my mouth, sir. I have the most reason to be glad of yours.
ROMAN. Well, let's go together.
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 4 — Antium. Before Aufidius’s house
paragraphs: Enter Coriolanus in mean apparel, disguised and muffled.

CORIOLANUS. A fine city, this Antium. City, it's I who made your widows. Many an heir of these handsome buildings I heard groan and drop dead in my wars. So don't recognize me now, or your wives with spits and your boys with stones will kill me in a puny battle.
Enter a Citizen.
God save you, sir.
CITIZEN. And you.
CORIOLANUS. Direct me, if you will, to where the great Aufidius lives. Is he in Antium?
CITIZEN. He is, and he's feasting the nobles of the state at his house tonight.
CORIOLANUS. Which is his house, please?
CITIZEN. This one right in front of you.
CORIOLANUS. Thank you, sir. Farewell.
[_Exit Citizen._]

Oh, world, how slippery your turns are! Friends who have sworn loyalty, whose two hearts seem to be one, whose hours, beds, meals and exercise are always shared, who are like twins in their inseparable love, will within the hour break out into the bitterest hatred over a quarrel about a tiny coin. And fiercest enemies, whose anger and plots have cost them sleep as each tried to catch the other, will by some chance, some trick not worth an egg, become dear friends and join their children in marriage. So it is with me. I hate my birthplace, and my love is given to this enemy town. I'll go in. If he kills me, he does fair justice. If he lets me by, I'll do his country service.
[_Exit._]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 5 — Antium. A hall in Aufidius’s house
paragraphs: Music plays. Enter a Servingman.
FIRST SERVINGMAN. Wine, wine, wine! What kind of service is this? I think our fellows are asleep.
[_Exit._]
Enter another Servingman.
SECOND SERVINGMAN. Where's Cotus? My master is calling for him. Cotus!
[_Exit._]
Enter Coriolanus.
CORIOLANUS. A fine house. The feast smells good, but I don't look like a guest.
Enter the First Servingman.
FIRST SERVINGMAN. What do you want, friend? Where are you from? There's no place for you here. Please go to the door.
[_Exit._]
CORIOLANUS. I deserve no better welcome for being Coriolanus.
Enter Second Servingman.
SECOND SERVINGMAN. Where are you from, sir? Has the porter got his eyes in his head, to let in such riffraff? Please, get out.
CORIOLANUS. Away!
SECOND SERVINGMAN. Away? You get away.
CORIOLANUS. Now you're being a nuisance.
SECOND SERVINGMAN. Are you so bold? You'll be spoken to soon enough.
Enter Third  Servingman; the First, entering, meets him.
THIRD SERVINGMAN. Who's this fellow?
FIRST SERVINGMAN. The strangest one I ever saw. I can't get him out of the house. Please call my master to him.
THIRD SERVINGMAN. What business do you have here, fellow? Please, clear out of the house.
CORIOLANUS. Just let me stand here. I won't harm your hearth.
THIRD SERVINGMAN. What are you?
CORIOLANUS. A gentleman.
THIRD SERVINGMAN. A wonderfully poor one.
CORIOLANUS. True, so I am.
THIRD SERVINGMAN. Please, poor gentleman, find some other place to stand. There's no place for you here. Please, clear out. Come on.
CORIOLANUS. Go do your job, and go fatten yourself on cold scraps.
[_Pushes him away from him_.]
THIRD SERVINGMAN. What, you won't go? Please, tell my master what a strange guest he has here.
SECOND SERVINGMAN. I will.
[_Exit._]
THIRD SERVINGMAN. Where do you live?
CORIOLANUS. Under the canopy of the sky.
THIRD SERVINGMAN. Under the canopy?
CORIOLANUS. Yes.
THIRD SERVINGMAN. Where's that?
CORIOLANUS. In the city of kites and crows.
THIRD SERVINGMAN. In the city of kites and crows? What an ass this man is! Then you live with jackdaws too?
CORIOLANUS. No, I don't serve your master.
THIRD SERVINGMAN. What, sir? Are you meddling with my master?
CORIOLANUS. Yes, it's an honester service than meddling with your mistress. You chatter and chatter. Go serve with your plate, and get out!
[_Beats him away_.]
[_Exit Third Servingman._]
Enter Aufidius with the Second Servingman.
AUFIDIUS. Where is this fellow?
SECOND SERVINGMAN. Here, sir. I'd have beaten him like a dog, but I didn't want to disturb the lords inside.
AUFIDIUS. Where do you come from? What do you want? What's your name? Why don't you speak? Speak, man. What's your name?
CORIOLANUS.
[_Removing his muffler_.] If, Tullus,
you still don't know me, and even seeing me you don't take me for the man I am, then necessity forces me to name myself.
AUFIDIUS. What is your name?
CORIOLANUS. A name unmusical to the Volscians' ears, and harsh in sound to yours.
AUFIDIUS. Say, what's your name? You look grim, and your face carries command in it. Though your rigging is torn, you show yourself a noble ship. What's your name?
CORIOLANUS. Get your brow ready to frown. Do you know me yet?
AUFIDIUS. I don't know you. Your name?

CORIOLANUS. My name is Caius Martius, who has done you in particular, and all the Volsces, great harm and damage. My surname Coriolanus bears witness to that. All my painful service, the extreme dangers, and the drops of blood I shed for my thankless country have been repaid with nothing but that surname, a good reminder and witness of the hatred and anger you ought to feel toward me. Only that name remains. The cruelty and envy of the people, allowed by our cowardly nobles, who have all deserted me, have devoured the rest. They let me be hooted out of Rome by the votes of slaves. Now this extremity has brought me to your hearth, not in hope of saving my life, don't mistake me. If I had feared death, I would have avoided you above all men in the world. I stand before you here purely out of spite, to be fully even with those who banished me. So if you have a heart eager for revenge, if you want to avenge your own particular wrongs and stop the wounds of shame that can be seen across your country, hurry, and make my misery serve your purpose. Use it so that my vengeful service proves a benefit to you, because I will fight against my festering country with the rage of all the devils below. But if you don't dare do this, and you're tired of trying more fortunes, then in a word, I too am weary of living any longer. I offer my throat to you and your old hatred. Not to cut it would make you a fool, since I have always pursued you with hate, drawn barrels of blood from your country's breast, and cannot live except to your shame, unless it is to do you service.

AUFIDIUS. Oh, Martius, Martius, each word you've spoken has pulled from my heart a root of old envy. If Jupiter spoke divine things from that cloud and said it was true, I wouldn't believe them more than I believe you, all-noble Martius. Let me wrap my arms around that body, against which my ash spear has broken a hundred times and scarred the moon with splinters. Here I embrace the anvil of my sword, and I compete as hotly and as nobly for your love as I ever did in ambitious strength against your courage. Know this first: I loved the girl I married. No man ever sighed more truly. But seeing you here, you noble thing, makes my rapt heart dance more than when I first saw my bride step over my threshold. Why, you Mars, I tell you, we have an army on foot, and I meant once more to cut your shield from your arm or lose my own arm for it. You have beaten me twelve separate times, and every night since I've dreamed of fights between you and me. We've been down together in my sleep, unbuckling helmets, gripping each other's throats, and I've woken half dead over nothing. Worthy Martius, if we had no other quarrel with Rome than that you're banished from it, we would muster everyone from twelve to seventy, and pour war into the bowels of ungrateful Rome and overwhelm it like a bold flood. Oh, come, go in, and take by the hand our friendly senators, who are here now, taking their leave of me. I'm prepared to march against your territories, though not against Rome itself.
CORIOLANUS. You bless me, gods!

AUFIDIUS. Therefore, most absolute sir, if you want to lead your own revenge, take half of my commission, and set down your own plans, as you're best qualified, since you know your country's strength and weakness. Decide whether to knock on the gates of Rome, or to strike roughly at its distant parts to frighten it before destroying it. But come in. Let me first present you to those who will say yes to your wishes. A thousand welcomes! And more a friend than you ever were an enemy. Yet, Martius, that was a lot. Your hand. Most welcome!
[_Exeunt Coriolanus and Aufidius._]
Two of the Servingmen come forward.
FIRST SERVINGMAN. What a strange change!
SECOND SERVINGMAN. By my hand, I meant to hit him with a cudgel, and yet my mind told me his clothes were giving a false report of him.
FIRST SERVINGMAN. What an arm he has! He spun me around with his finger and thumb like you'd set up a spinning top.
SECOND SERVINGMAN. No, I knew by his face that there was something in him. He had, sir, a kind of face, I thought. I can't say how to describe it.
FIRST SERVINGMAN. He did, looking like, well, I'll be hanged if I didn't think there was more in him than I could put into thought.
SECOND SERVINGMAN. So did I, I'll swear. He's simply the rarest man in the world.
FIRST SERVINGMAN. I think he is. But you know a man who's a greater soldier than he is.
SECOND SERVINGMAN. Who, my master?
FIRST SERVINGMAN. No, never mind that.
SECOND SERVINGMAN. Worth six of him.
FIRST SERVINGMAN. No, not so, either. But I take him to be the greater soldier.
SECOND SERVINGMAN. Well, look, you can't really say that. For the defense of a town our general is excellent.
FIRST SERVINGMAN. Yes, and for an assault too.
Enter the Third Servingman.
THIRD SERVINGMAN. Oh, slaves, I can tell you news, news, you rascals!
FIRST and SECOND SERVINGMAN. What, what, what? Let us share it.
THIRD SERVINGMAN. Of all nations, I wouldn't be a Roman. I'd as soon be a condemned man.
FIRST and SECOND SERVINGMAN. Why? Why?
THIRD SERVINGMAN. Why, here's the man who used to thrash our general, Caius Martius.
FIRST SERVINGMAN. Why do you say "thrash our general"?
THIRD SERVINGMAN. I don't say "thrash our general," but he was always good enough for him.
SECOND SERVINGMAN. Come on, we're fellows and friends. He was always too hard for him. I've heard him say so himself.
FIRST SERVINGMAN. He was too hard for him outright, to tell the truth of it, before Corioles. He slashed him and scored him like a piece of meat for the grill.
SECOND SERVINGMAN. If he'd had a taste for human flesh, he might have boiled and eaten him too.
FIRST SERVINGMAN. But what more of your news?

THIRD SERVINGMAN. Why, he's made so much of in there, as if he were Mars's son and heir. He's set at the top of the table. None of the senators asks him a question without standing bareheaded before him. Our general himself treats him like a sweetheart, blesses himself with his hand, and rolls up the whites of his eyes at his talk. But the bottom of the news is that our general is cut in the middle and is only half of what he was yesterday, because the other man has half, by the request and grant of the whole table. He says he'll go and drag the porter of Rome's gates by the ears. He'll mow everything down before him and leave his path stripped bare.
SECOND SERVINGMAN. And he's as likely to do it as any man I can imagine.

THIRD SERVINGMAN. Do it? He will do it! For look, sir, he has as many friends as enemies. And those friends, sir, as it were, didn't dare, look, sir, show themselves, as we say, his friends while he was in directitude.
FIRST SERVINGMAN. Directitude? What's that?
THIRD SERVINGMAN. But when they see, sir, his crest up again, and the man in blood, they'll come out of their burrows like rabbits after rain, and revel with him.
FIRST SERVINGMAN. But when does this go forward?
THIRD SERVINGMAN. Tomorrow, today, right now. You'll have the drum struck up this afternoon. It's like part of their feast, and will be carried out before they wipe their lips.
SECOND SERVINGMAN. Why then, we'll have a stirring world again. This peace is good for nothing but rusting iron, multiplying tailors, and breeding ballad-makers.

FIRST SERVINGMAN. Give me war, I say. It beats peace as far as day beats night. It's lively to walk in, loud, and full of outlet. Peace is a real apoplexy, a lethargy; muffled, deaf, sleepy, numb; a father of more bastard children than war is a destroyer of men.
SECOND SERVINGMAN. That's so, and just as war may in some sense be called a rapist, it can't be denied that peace is a great maker of cuckolds.
FIRST SERVINGMAN. Yes, and it makes men hate one another.
THIRD SERVINGMAN. There's a reason: because then they need one another less. War for my money! I hope to see Romans as cheap as Volscians. They are rising; they are rising.
ALL. In, in, in, in!
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 6 — Rome. A public place
paragraphs: Enter the two Tribunes. Sicinius and Brutus.

SICINIUS. We hear nothing of him, and we needn't fear him. His cures are tame ones: the present peace and the quiet of the people, who before were in a wild rush. Here we make his friends blush that the world goes well. They would rather, even though they suffer for it themselves, see quarreling crowds pestering the streets than see our tradesmen singing in their shops and going about their work in friendship.
BRUTUS. We stood up to him in good time.
Enter Menenius.
Is this Menenius?
SICINIUS. It's him, it's him. Oh, he has grown very kind lately. Hail, sir!
MENENIUS. Hail to you both.
SICINIUS. Your Coriolanus isn't much missed except by his friends. The commonwealth stands, and would stand even if he were angrier about it.
MENENIUS. All's well, and might have been much better if he could have bent with the times.
SICINIUS. Where is he, do you hear?
MENENIUS. No, I hear nothing. His mother and his wife hear nothing from him.
Enter three or four Citizens.
ALL CITIZENS. The gods preserve you both!
SICINIUS. Good evening, our neighbors.
BRUTUS. Good evening to you all, good evening to you all.
FIRST CITIZEN. We, our wives and our children, on our knees, are bound to pray for you both.
SICINIUS. Live and thrive!
BRUTUS. Farewell, kind neighbors. We wish Coriolanus had loved you as we did.
CITIZENS. Now the gods keep you!
BOTH TRIBUNES. Farewell, farewell.
[_Exeunt Citizens._]
SICINIUS. This is a happier and more decent time than when these fellows ran about the streets crying chaos.
BRUTUS. Caius Martius was a worthy officer in the war, but he was insolent, overcome with pride, ambitious, and self-loving beyond all belief.
SICINIUS. And he aimed at ruling alone on one throne, without help.
MENENIUS. I don't think so.
SICINIUS. If he had gone out as consul, we would by now have found it so, to our great sorrow.
BRUTUS. The gods have prevented it well, and Rome sits safe and quiet without him.
Enter an Aedile.

AEDILE. Worthy tribunes, there is a slave we've put in prison who reports that the Volsces have entered Roman territory with two separate armies. With the deepest malice of war, they are destroying everything in front of them.

MENENIUS. It's Aufidius. When he heard of our Martius's banishment, he pushed his horns out into the world again. They had been pulled back into their shell while Martius stood up for Rome, and he didn't dare peep out once.
SICINIUS. Come, why do you talk about Martius?
BRUTUS. Go see this rumor-monger whipped. It can't be that the Volsces dare break with us.

MENENIUS. Can't be? We have records that it very well can, and there have been three examples of the same within my lifetime. But question the fellow before you punish him, about where he heard this. Otherwise you may end up whipping your source of information and beating the messenger who tells you to beware of what is to be dreaded.
SICINIUS. Don't tell me. I know this can't be.
BRUTUS. Not possible.
Enter a Messenger.
MESSENGER. The nobles are all going in great earnest to the Senate House. Some news has come that changes their faces.
SICINIUS. It's this slave. Go whip him before the people's eyes. His stirring things up is nothing but his own report.
MESSENGER. Yes, worthy sir, but the slave's report is backed up, and more, something more frightening, is being delivered.
SICINIUS. What more frightening?

MESSENGER. It's being said openly by many mouths, though how probable it is I don't know, that Martius, joined with Aufidius, leads an army against Rome. He vows revenge as wide as the space between the youngest thing and the oldest.
SICINIUS. This is most likely!
BRUTUS. It's put out only so that the weaker sort may wish good Martius home again.
SICINIUS. That's exactly the trick.
MENENIUS. This is unlikely. He and Aufidius can no more be reconciled than the most violent opposites.
Enter a Second Messenger.

SECOND MESSENGER. You are sent for to the Senate. A fearsome army, led by Caius Martius and allied with Aufidius, is raging through our territories. They have already overrun their way, burned with fire and seized what lay before them.
Enter Cominius.
COMINIUS. Oh, you have done fine work!
MENENIUS. What news? What news?
COMINIUS. You have helped to rape your own daughters, to have the city's lead roofs melted down on your heads, and to see your wives dishonored right under your noses —
MENENIUS. What's the news? What's the news?
COMINIUS. Your temples burned down to their mortar, and your rights, which you stood so firmly on, shrunk to the size of an auger's hole.
MENENIUS. Please now, your news? You have done fine work, I fear. Please, your news? If Martius should be joined with the Volscians —

COMINIUS. If? He is their god. He leads them like a thing made by some other deity than Nature, who shapes men better. And they follow him against us brats with no less confidence than boys chasing summer butterflies or butchers killing flies.
MENENIUS. You have done fine work, you and your apron-men, you who stood so much on the votes of tradesmen and the breath of garlic-eaters!
COMINIUS. He'll shake your Rome down around your ears.
MENENIUS. As Hercules shook down ripe fruit. You have done fine work.
BRUTUS. But is this true, sir?

COMINIUS. Yes, and you'll turn pale before you find it otherwise. All the regions revolt cheerfully, and those who resist are mocked for their brave ignorance and die as steadfast fools. Who can blame him? Your enemies and his find something to admire in him.
MENENIUS. We are all ruined unless the noble man has mercy.

COMINIUS. Who will ask it of him? The tribunes can't do it, for shame. The people deserve as much pity from him as the wolf gives the shepherds. As for his best friends, if they said "Be good to Rome," they would be charging him just as those would who had earned his hatred, and so they would look like enemies.

MENENIUS. It's true. If he were putting to my house the torch that would burn it down, I wouldn't have the face to say "Please, stop." You have made a fine mess, you and your trades! You have crafted well!
COMINIUS. You have brought on Rome a trembling such as never before was so beyond help.
TRIBUNES. Don't say we brought it.
MENENIUS. What? Was it we? We loved him, but like beasts and cowardly nobles we gave way to your swarms, who hooted him out of the city.

COMINIUS. But I fear they'll roar him back in again. Tullus Aufidius, the second name among men, obeys his orders as if he were his officer. Desperation is all the strategy, strength and defense that Rome can make against them.
Enter a troop of Citizens.

MENENIUS. Here come the swarms. And is Aufidius with him? You are the ones who made the air unwholesome when you threw up your stinking, greasy caps, hooting at Coriolanus's exile. Now he's coming, and there's not a hair on a soldier's head that won't prove a whip. As many fools' heads as you threw caps up for, he will knock down, and pay you for your votes. It doesn't matter. If he could burn us all into one coal, we would deserve it.
ALL CITIZENS. Truly, we hear fearful news.
FIRST CITIZEN. For my own part, when I said banish him, I said it was a pity.
SECOND CITIZEN. And so did I.
THIRD CITIZEN. And so did I. And to tell the truth, so did very many of us. What we did, we did for the best. And though we willingly agreed to his banishment, it was still against our will.
COMINIUS. You are fine things, you votes!
MENENIUS. You have done fine work, you and your pack! Shall we go to the Capitol?
COMINIUS. Oh, yes, what else?
[_Exeunt Cominius and Menenius._]
SICINIUS. Go, masters, get yourselves home. Don't be dismayed. These are a faction that would be glad to have this be true, though they seem to fear it. Go home, and show no sign of fear.
FIRST CITIZEN. The gods be good to us! Come, masters, let's go home. I always said we were in the wrong when we banished him.
SECOND CITIZEN. So did we all. But come, let's go home.
[_Exeunt Citizens._]
BRUTUS. I don't like this news.
SICINIUS. Nor I.
BRUTUS. Let's go to the Capitol. I wish half my wealth could buy this back as a lie!
SICINIUS. Please, let's go.
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 7 — A camp at a short distance from Rome
paragraphs: Enter Aufidius with his Lieutenant.
AUFIDIUS. Do they still flock to the Roman?

LIEUTENANT. I don't know what witchcraft is in him, but your soldiers use his name like the blessing before a meal, as their talk at table and their thanks at the end. And you are put in the shade in this campaign, sir, even by your own men.

AUFIDIUS. I can't help it now, unless by taking action I cripple the foot of our whole plan. He carries himself more proudly, even toward me, than I thought he would when I first embraced him. Yet his nature never changes in that, and I must excuse what can't be mended.
LIEUTENANT. Yet I wish, sir, I mean for your own sake, that you had not shared command with him, but had either carried out the campaign yourself or else left it entirely to him.

AUFIDIUS. I understand you well, and be sure of this: when he comes to his reckoning, he doesn't know what I can bring against him. It seems, and he thinks so, and it's no less plain to the common eye, that he conducts everything well, shows good management for the Volscian state, fights like a dragon, and succeeds as soon as he draws his sword. Yet he has left undone the thing that will break his neck or endanger mine, whenever we come to our reckoning.
LIEUTENANT. Sir, I beg you, do you think he'll take Rome?

AUFIDIUS. Every place yields to him before he sits down to besiege it, and the nobility of Rome are his. The senators and patricians love him too. The tribunes are no soldiers, and their people will be as rash in calling him back as they were hasty to expel him. I think he'll be to Rome as the osprey is to the fish, which it takes by the right of nature's rule. First, he was a noble servant to them, but he could not carry his honors evenly. Whether it was pride, which from daily good fortune always taints the happy man, or a defect of judgment, failing to manage the chances he was master of, or his nature, which could not be other than one thing, not moving from the helmet to the cushion of office but commanding peace with the same sternness and manner as he ruled the war: one of these, since he has a taste of all of them, though not all, for I'll go that far in clearing him, made him feared, so hated, and so banished. But he has a merit that he chokes in the very telling. So our virtues lie in how the time interprets them. And power, most praiseworthy in its own eyes, has no tomb so plain as a chair from which to praise what it has done. One fire drives out another fire, one nail another nail. Rights fail by rights, strengths are beaten by strengths. Come, let's go. When, Caius, Rome is yours, you are the poorest of all, and then soon you will be mine.
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 1 — Rome. A public place
paragraphs: Enter Menenius, Cominius, Sicinius, Brutus (the two Tribunes), with others.

MENENIUS. No, I won't go. You heard what he said, who was once his general and loved him dearly. He called me father, but what of that? You go, you who banished him. A mile before his tent, fall down and crawl on your knees to win his mercy. No, if he played coy when Cominius spoke to him, I'll stay at home.
COMINIUS. He wouldn't even seem to know me.
MENENIUS. Do you hear that?

COMINIUS. Yet one time he did call me by my name. I appealed to our old acquaintance and the drops of blood we have shed together. He wouldn't answer to "Coriolanus." He forbade all names. He was a kind of nothing, without a title, until he had forged himself a name in the fire of burning Rome.
MENENIUS. Why, so. You have done fine work! A pair of tribunes who have wrecked Rome to make coals cheap! A noble memory!
COMINIUS. I reminded him how royal it is to pardon when it is least expected. He replied that it was only a bare petition from a state to someone it had punished.
MENENIUS. Very well. Could he say less?

COMINIUS. I offered to awaken his regard for his private friends. His answer to me was that he couldn't stop to pick them out of a pile of foul, moldy chaff. He said it was folly to leave one poor grain or two unburnt and still smell the offense.

MENENIUS. One poor grain or two! I am one of those! His mother, his wife, his child, and this brave fellow here, we are the grains. You are the moldy chaff, and you are smelled above the moon. We must be burned for your sake.

SICINIUS. No, please, be patient. If you refuse your help in this time when help was never so needed, at least don't reproach us for our distress. But surely, if you would plead for your country, your good tongue, more than any army we can raise on the spot, might stop our countryman.
MENENIUS. No, I won't meddle.
SICINIUS. Please, go to him.
MENENIUS. What should I do?
BRUTUS. Only try what your love for Rome can do with Martius.
MENENIUS. Well, and suppose Martius sends me back as he sent Cominius back, unheard? What then? I'd be just a disappointed friend, shot through with grief at his unkindness. Say it turns out so?
SICINIUS. Even so, Rome will thank your good will in proportion to how well you meant it.

MENENIUS. I'll undertake it. I think he'll hear me. Yet his biting his lip and humming at good Cominius discourages me a lot. He wasn't approached at a good time. He hadn't dined. When the veins are unfilled, our blood is cold, and then we sulk in the morning and are unfit to give or to forgive. But when we have stuffed these pipes and channels of our blood with wine and food, we have suppler souls than in our priestlike fasts. So I'll watch him until he's fed enough for my request, and then I'll set upon him.
BRUTUS. You know the very road into his kindness and can't lose your way.
MENENIUS. In good faith, I'll test him, however it turns out. I'll soon know how I've succeeded.
[_Exit._]
COMINIUS. He'll never listen to him.
SICINIUS. No?

COMINIUS. I tell you, he sits in gold, his eye as red as if it would burn Rome, and his injury is the jailer of his pity. I knelt before him. He said "Rise" very faintly, and dismissed me like this, with his silent hand. What he would do, he sent in writing after me. What he would not do, he bound with an oath not to yield to, except on his conditions. So all hope is vain, unless it comes through his noble mother and his wife, who, as I hear, mean to plead with him for mercy to his country. So let's go from here and hurry them on with our fair entreaties.
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 2 — An Advanced post of the Volscian camp before Rome
paragraphs: Enter Menenius to the Watch, or Guard.
FIRST WATCH. Stop! Where are you from?
SECOND WATCH. Halt, and go back.
MENENIUS. You guard like men, and that's good. But with your permission, I am an officer of state and I've come to speak with Coriolanus.
FIRST WATCH. From where?
MENENIUS. From Rome.
FIRST WATCH. You may not pass. You must go back. Our general will hear nothing more from there.
SECOND WATCH. You'll see your Rome embraced by fire before you speak with Coriolanus.
MENENIUS. My good friends, if you have heard your general talk of Rome and of his friends there, the odds are heavily in favor that my name has reached your ears. It is Menenius.
FIRST WATCH. Be it so. Go back. The power of your name doesn't carry here.

MENENIUS. I tell you, fellow, your general is my dear friend. I have been the book of his good deeds, from which men have read his unequaled fame, happily enlarged. For I have always vouched for my friends, and he is the chief of them, to the full size that the truth would allow without slipping. Indeed, sometimes, like a bowl on tricky ground, I have rolled past the mark, and in his praise I have almost stamped a lie as true. So, fellow, I must have leave to pass.

FIRST WATCH. Truly, sir, if you had told as many lies on his behalf as you have uttered words on your own, you still wouldn't pass here, no, even if lying were as virtuous as living chastely. So go back.
MENENIUS. Please, fellow, remember my name is Menenius, always a partisan on the side of your general.
SECOND WATCH. However much you have been his liar, as you say you have, I am a man who, telling the truth under him, must say you cannot pass. So go back.
MENENIUS. Has he dined, can you tell? I wouldn't want to speak with him until after dinner.
FIRST WATCH. You are a Roman, are you?
MENENIUS. I am, as your general is.

FIRST WATCH. Then you should hate Rome as he does. When you have pushed out of your gates the very man who defended them, and in a violent, mob-driven ignorance have handed your enemy your shield, can you think to face his revenge with the easy groans of old women, the virginal palms of your daughters, or the shaky pleading of such a decayed old dotard as you seem to be? Can you think to blow out the fire intended for your city, which is ready to blaze, with such weak breath as this? No, you are deceived. So go back to Rome and prepare for your execution. You are condemned. Our general has sworn you out of reprieve and pardon.
MENENIUS. Fellow, if your captain knew I were here, he would treat me with respect.
SECOND WATCH. Come, my captain doesn't know you.
MENENIUS. I mean your general.
FIRST WATCH. My general doesn't care about you. Back, I say, go, or I'll let out your half pint of blood. Back! That's the most you have. Back!
MENENIUS. No, but fellow, fellow —
Enter Coriolanus with Aufidius.
CORIOLANUS. What's the matter?

MENENIUS. Now, you scoundrel, I'll tell you a thing or two. You'll learn now that I am held in respect. You'll see that a petty Jack of a guard can't keep me from my son Coriolanus. Judge just by how he receives me whether you're not in the state of hanging or of some death longer to watch and crueler to suffer. Look now, and faint at what's about to come upon you. [_to Coriolanus_.] The glorious gods sit in hourly council about your particular welfare and love you no worse than your old father Menenius does! Oh, my son, my son! You are preparing fire for us. Look, here's water to put it out. I was hard to move to come to you. But being sure that no one but me could move you, I have been blown out of your gates with sighs, and I beg you to pardon Rome and your begging countrymen. May the good gods calm your wrath and turn the dregs of it upon this rascal here, this fellow who, like a block of wood, has denied me access to you.
CORIOLANUS. Away!
MENENIUS. What? Away?

CORIOLANUS. Wife, mother, child, I don't know them. My business is now in the service of others. Though my revenge is properly mine to give, my mercy lies in Volscian hearts. As for our having been close, ungrateful forgetfulness will poison it sooner than pity will note how close we were. So be gone. My ears against your pleas are stronger than your gates against my force. Yet, because I loved you, take this along. I wrote it for your sake,
[_He gives Menenius a paper._]
and would have sent it. Another word, Menenius, and I won't hear you speak. This man, Aufidius, was my beloved friend in Rome. Yet you see how it is.
AUFIDIUS. You keep a constant temper.
[_They exit._]
[_The Guard and Menenius remain._]
FIRST WATCH. Now, sir, is your name Menenius?
SECOND WATCH. It's a spell, you see, of much power. You know the way home again.
FIRST WATCH. Do you hear how we are scolded for keeping your Greatness back?
SECOND WATCH. What reason do you think I have to faint?

MENENIUS. I care neither for the world nor your general. As for such things as you, I can hardly think you exist, you're so slight. A man who has the will to die by his own hand doesn't fear it from another. Let your general do his worst. As for you, go on being what you are, for a long time, and may your misery grow with your age! I say to you what was said to me: away!
[_Exit._]
FIRST WATCH. A noble fellow, I'll warrant.
SECOND WATCH. The worthy fellow is our general. He is the rock, the oak that can't be shaken by wind.
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 3 — The tent of Coriolanus
paragraphs: Enter Coriolanus and Aufidius.
CORIOLANUS. Tomorrow we will set up our army in front of the walls of Rome. My partner in this campaign, you must tell the Volscian lords how plainly I have handled this business.

AUFIDIUS. You have thought only of their interests. You have shut your ears to the general plea from Rome. You have never let in a private whisper, not even from friends who thought they could count on you.

CORIOLANUS. This last old man, whom I sent back to Rome with a broken heart, loved me more than a father would. He all but made a god of me. Their last resort was to send him. Out of old love for him, I offered once more the first terms, though I treated him sourly. They refused those terms and cannot accept them now. I did it only to honor him, since he thought he could do more. I have given way a very little. From now on I will listen to no more embassies or pleas, whether from the state or from private friends.
[_Shout within._]
Ha? What shout is this? Shall I be tempted to break my vow at the very moment I make it? I will not.
Enter Virgilia, Volumnia, Valeria, young Martius with attendants.

My wife comes first, then the honored mold that shaped this body, and in her hand the grandchild of her blood. But away, affection! All bonds and privileges of nature, break! Let it be a virtue to be stubborn. What is that curtsy worth? Or those dove's eyes, which can make gods break their oaths? I am melting, and I am made of no stronger earth than other men. My mother bows to me, as if Mount Olympus were to nod in pleading to a molehill. And my young boy has a look of begging that Nature herself cries out, "Don't refuse!" Let the Volsces plough Rome and harrow Italy. I will never be such a gosling as to obey instinct. I will stand as if a man made himself, and knew no other family.
VIRGILIA. My lord and husband.
CORIOLANUS. These eyes are not the same ones I wore in Rome.
VIRGILIA. The sorrow that has changed us like this makes you think so.
CORIOLANUS. Like a poor actor, I have forgotten my part, and I am lost, to my total disgrace. Best part of my flesh, forgive my harshness, but do not say, because of it, "Forgive our Romans."
[_They kiss._]

Oh, a kiss as long as my exile, as sweet as my revenge! Now, by the jealous queen of heaven, the kiss I took away from you, dear, my true lip has kept pure ever since. You gods! I chatter, and leave unsaluted the most noble mother in the world. Sink, my knee, into the earth;
[_Kneels._]
show more of a deep son's duty than common sons do.
VOLUMNIA. Oh, stand up, blessed one,
[_He rises_.]
while I, on no softer cushion than the flint, kneel before you and show my duty in the wrong way, as if the roles of child and parent had been mistaken all this time.
[_She kneels._]
CORIOLANUS. What is this? Your knees to me? To your scolded son?
[_He raises her up._]

Then let the pebbles on the hungry beach flick up at the stars! Let the mutinous winds hurl the proud cedars against the fiery sun, killing impossibility by making what cannot be done look like easy work.
VOLUMNIA. You are my warrior. I helped to shape you. Do you know this lady?
CORIOLANUS. The noble sister of Publicola, the moon of Rome, chaste as the icicle that is frozen from purest snow by the frost and hangs on Diana's temple! Dear Valeria.
VOLUMNIA. This is a poor miniature of you, which in the course of time may grow to look like all of you.

CORIOLANUS. May the god of soldiers, with the consent of supreme Jupiter, fill your thoughts with nobility, so that you prove to be beyond shame's wounding, and stand firm in the wars like a great seamark, withstanding every gust and saving those who look to you.
VOLUMNIA.
[_To young Martius_.] Your knee, boy.
[_He kneels._]
CORIOLANUS. That's my brave boy!
VOLUMNIA. This same boy, your wife, this lady, and I myself are asking something of you.
[_Young Martius rises._]

CORIOLANUS. I beg you, be quiet. Or, if you do ask, remember this first: you must not count as refusals the things I have sworn not to grant. Do not tell me to dismiss my soldiers or to bargain again with Rome's tradesmen. Do not tell me how I seem unnatural. Do not ask me to soften my rages and revenges with your colder reasons.

VOLUMNIA. Oh, no more, no more! You have said you will not grant us anything. We have nothing else to ask for but what you already refuse. Still, we will ask, so that if you fail our request, the blame may hang on your hardness. So hear us.
CORIOLANUS. Aufidius, and you Volsces, listen, for we will hear nothing from Rome in private. What is your request?

VOLUMNIA. If we were silent and said nothing, our clothes and the state of our bodies would reveal what kind of life we have led since your exile. Think for yourself how much more unfortunate than all living women we are, coming here. The sight of you should make our eyes flow with joy and our hearts dance with comfort. Instead it forces them to weep and shake with fear and sorrow, making the mother, wife and child see the son, the husband and the father tearing his country's guts out. And for us poor women, your enmity is the deadliest of all. You bar us from our prayers to the gods, a comfort everyone enjoys but us. For how can we, alas, how can we pray for our country, to which we are bound, together with your victory, to which we are also bound? Alas, either we must lose our country, our dear nurse, or lose you, our comfort in the country. Whichever side wins, we must find disaster, even if we got our wish. For you must either be led through our streets in chains as a foreign traitor, or else march in triumph over your country's ruin and carry off the victor's palm for having bravely shed your wife's and children's blood. As for me, son, I do not intend to wait for fortune until these wars are decided. If I cannot persuade you to show a noble mercy to both sides rather than seek the destruction of one, you will march to attack your country no sooner than you will tread, trust me, you will not, on your mother's womb, which brought you into this world.
VIRGILIA. Yes, and on mine, which bore you this boy to keep your name alive through time.
YOUNG MARTIUS. He shall not tread on me. I'll run away until I'm bigger, but then I'll fight.
CORIOLANUS. A man who will not show a woman's tenderness must not look at a child's or a woman's face. I have sat too long.
[_He rises._]

VOLUMNIA. No, don't go from us like this. If our request were meant to save the Romans by destroying the Volsces you serve, you could condemn us as poison to your honor. But no, our plea is that you reconcile them. Then the Volsces can say, "We showed this mercy," and the Romans, "We received this," and each side can hail you and cry, "Blessed be the man who made this peace!" You know, great son, that the end of war is uncertain, but this much is certain. If you conquer Rome, the reward you reap will be a name whose mention will be followed by curses. Its record will read: "The man was noble, but with his last attempt he wiped it out. He destroyed his country, and his name remains hated by the age that follows." Speak to me, son. You have aimed at the fine strains of honor, to imitate the graces of the gods, to tear the wide cheeks of the air with thunder and yet load your sulphur with a bolt that would only split an oak. Why don't you speak? Do you think it honorable for a noble man to keep remembering wrongs forever? Daughter, you speak. He doesn't care about your weeping. Speak, boy. Perhaps your childishness will move him more than our reasons can. There is no man in the world more bound to his mother, yet here he lets me babble like a man in the stocks. You have never in your life shown your dear mother any courtesy, though she, a poor hen, fond of no second brood, has clucked you off to the wars and safely home, loaded with honor. Say my request is unjust and push me away. But if it is not, then you are not honest, and the gods will plague you for holding back from me the duty that belongs to a mother. He turns away. Down, ladies! Let us shame him with our knees. There is more pride than pity for our prayers in his surname Coriolanus. Down! That's the end.
[_They kneel._]

This is the last. So we will go home to Rome and die among our neighbors. No, look at us. This boy, who cannot tell what he wants, but kneels and holds up his hands to keep us company, argues our petition with more force than you have to refuse it. Come, let us go.
[_They rise._]

This fellow had a Volscian for his mother, his wife is in Corioles, and his child is like him only by chance. Still, give us our dismissal. I will be silent until our city is on fire, and then I'll speak a little.
[_He holds her by the hand, silent._]

CORIOLANUS. Oh mother, mother! What have you done? Look, the heavens open, the gods look down, and they laugh at this unnatural scene. Oh my mother, mother, oh! You have won a happy victory for Rome. But for your son, believe it, oh, believe it! you have prevailed over him most dangerously, if not fatally. But let it come. Aufidius, though I cannot wage a true war, I'll arrange a fitting peace. Now, good Aufidius, if you were in my place, would you have listened to a mother less? Or granted less, Aufidius?
AUFIDIUS. I was moved by it too.

CORIOLANUS. I dare swear you were. And, sir, it is no small thing to make my eyes sweat with pity. But, good sir, advise me what peace you'll make. For my part, I will not go to Rome. I'll go back with you. Please stand by me in this cause. Oh mother! Wife!
[_He speaks with them aside._]
AUFIDIUS.
[_Aside_.] I am glad you have set your mercy and your honor
at odds within you. Out of that I'll build myself a return to my former fortune.
CORIOLANUS.
[_To the Women_.] Yes, soon.

But we'll drink together, and you shall carry back better proof than words, which we, on the same terms, will have countersealed. Come, enter with us. Ladies, you deserve to have a temple built for you. All the swords in Italy, and her allied armies, could not have made this peace.
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 4 — Rome. A public place
paragraphs: Enter Menenius and Sicinius.
MENENIUS. Do you see that corner of the Capitol over there, that cornerstone?
SICINIUS. Why, what about it?

MENENIUS. If you can shift it with your little finger, there is some hope that the ladies of Rome, especially his mother, may win him over. But I say there is no hope in it. Our throats are sentenced and are only waiting for the execution.
SICINIUS. Is it possible that so short a time can change a man's nature?
MENENIUS. There is a difference between a grub and a butterfly, yet your butterfly was a grub. This Martius has grown from man to dragon. He has wings. He is more than a creeping thing.
SICINIUS. He loved his mother dearly.

MENENIUS. So he did me, and he remembers his mother no more now than an eight-year-old horse does. The sourness of his face turns ripe grapes sour. When he walks, he moves like a siege engine, and the ground shrinks under his tread. He can pierce a breastplate with his eye, talks like a funeral bell, and his hum is a cannonade. He sits on his throne like something made for Alexander. What he orders to be done is finished as soon as he orders it. He lacks nothing of a god but eternity and a heaven to sit enthroned in.
SICINIUS. Yes, mercy, if you describe him truly.

MENENIUS. I paint him true to character. Just watch what mercy his mother will bring out of him. There is no more mercy in him than there is milk in a male tiger. Our poor city will find that out, and all of it is because of you.
SICINIUS. The gods be good to us.
MENENIUS. No, in a case like this the gods will not be good to us. When we banished him, we showed them no respect. Now that he is returning to break our necks, they show us none.
Enter a Messenger.

MESSENGER. Sir, if you want to save your life, run to your house. The plebeians have got your fellow tribune and are dragging him up and down, all swearing that if the Roman ladies do not bring back comfort, they will put him to death by inches.
Enter another Messenger.
SICINIUS. What's the news?

SECOND MESSENGER. Good news, good news! The ladies have won. The Volscians have withdrawn their camp and Martius is gone. A happier day has never yet greeted Rome, no, not even the expulsion of the Tarquins.
SICINIUS. Friend, are you certain this is true? Is it quite certain?

SECOND MESSENGER. As certain as I know the sun is fire. Where have you been hiding, that you doubt it? A swollen tide never rushed through an arch as fast as the comforted people through the gates. Why, listen!
[_Trumpets, hautboys, drums beat, all together._]
The trumpets, sackbuts, psalteries and fifes, tabors and cymbals, and the shouting Romans make the sun dance. Listen!
[_A shout within._]

MENENIUS. This is good news. I will go to meet the ladies. This Volumnia is worth a whole city full of consuls, senators and patricians, and a sea and land full of tribunes like you.
