You have prayed well today. This morning I would not have given a farthing for ten thousand of your throats. Hear how they rejoice!
[_Sound still with the shouts._]
SICINIUS. First, the gods bless you for your news. Next, accept my thanks.
SECOND MESSENGER. Sir, we all have great reason to give great thanks.
SICINIUS. Are they near the city?
MESSENGER. Almost at the point of entering.
SICINIUS. We'll meet them, and help the joy along.
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 5 — Rome. A street near the gate
paragraphs: Enter two Senators, with Ladies (Volumnia, Virgilia, Valeria) passing over the stage, with other Lords.

SENATOR. Behold our patroness, the life of Rome! Call all your tribes together, praise the gods, and make triumphant fires. Strew flowers before them. Unshout the noise that banished Martius. Call him back with the welcome of his mother. Cry, "Welcome, ladies, welcome!"
ALL. Welcome, ladies, welcome!
[_A flourish with drums and trumpets._]
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 6 — Antium. A public place
paragraphs: Enter Tullus Aufidius with Attendants.
AUFIDIUS. Go tell the lords of the city I am here. Give them this paper.
[_He gives them a paper_.]

When they have read it, tell them to come to the marketplace, where, in their hearing and in the commons' hearing, I will vouch for its truth. The man I accuse has by now entered the city gates and means to appear before the people, hoping to clear himself with words. Go quickly.
[_Exeunt Attendants._]
Enter three or four Conspirators of Aufidius's faction.
Most welcome!
FIRST CONSPIRATOR. How is it with our general?
AUFIDIUS. Just like a man poisoned by his own alms and killed by his own charity.
SECOND CONSPIRATOR. Most noble sir, if you still hold the same intention for which you wanted us as partners, we will free you from your great danger.
AUFIDIUS. Sir, I cannot tell. We must proceed as we find the people.
THIRD CONSPIRATOR. The people will stay uncertain as long as there is a quarrel between the two of you. But the fall of either makes the survivor heir to everything.

AUFIDIUS. I know it, and my pretext for striking at him will bear a good reading. I raised him up, and I pledged my honor for his loyalty. Once he was so lifted, he watered his new plants with the dews of flattery and so seduced my friends. To that end he bent his nature, which had never been known to be anything but rough, unbending and free.
THIRD CONSPIRATOR. Sir, his stubbornness when he stood for consul, which he lost for lack of stooping —

AUFIDIUS. That I was about to speak of. Banished for it, he came to my hearth and offered his throat to my knife. I took him in and made him joint servant with me. I gave him his way in all his desires. I even let him choose, out of my ranks, the best and freshest men to carry out his plans. I served his designs in my own person. I helped to reap the fame that he then made all his own. I took some pride in doing myself this wrong, until at last I seemed his follower, not his partner. And he paid me with his mere favor, as if I had been a hired soldier.
FIRST CONSPIRATOR. So he did, my lord. The army marveled at it. And in the end, when he had carried Rome and we expected no less spoil than glory —

AUFIDIUS. There was the thing for which my sinews shall be stretched against him. At a few drops of women's tears, which are as cheap as lies, he sold the blood and labor of our great enterprise. Therefore he shall die, and I'll renew myself in his fall. But listen!
[_Drums and trumpets sound, with great shouts of the people._]
FIRST CONSPIRATOR. You entered your native town like a courier, and had no welcome home. But he returns splitting the air with noise.
SECOND CONSPIRATOR. And the patient fools, whose children he has killed, tear their base throats giving him glory.

THIRD CONSPIRATOR. So strike at your advantage. Before he explains himself or moves the people with what he wants to say, let him feel your sword, and we will back you. When he lies stretched out, your account of him, once told, will bury his reasons along with his body.
AUFIDIUS. Say no more. Here come the lords.
Enter the Lords of the city.
ALL LORDS. You are most welcome home.
AUFIDIUS. I have not deserved it. But, worthy lords, have you read carefully what I wrote to you?
ALL LORDS. We have.

FIRST LORD. And we grieve to hear it. As for the faults he made before the last, I think they might have been settled with easy fines. But to end where he should have begun, and give away the benefit of our levies, answering us with our own expense, making a treaty where there was a yielding, this admits no excuse.
Enter Coriolanus marching with Drum and Colours, the Commoners being with him.
AUFIDIUS. He approaches. You shall hear him.

CORIOLANUS. Hail, lords! I have returned your soldier, no more infected with love of my country than when I left here, but still serving under your great command. You should know that I have succeeded in my attempt, and have led your wars with bloody passage right up to the gates of Rome. The spoils we have brought home more than outweigh a full third part of the cost of the campaign. We have made peace with no less honor to the Antiates than shame to the Romans. Here we hand over, signed by the Consuls and patricians and sealed by the Senate, what we have agreed on.
[_He offers the lords a paper._]
AUFIDIUS. Do not read it, noble lords. Instead, tell the traitor, the worst kind of traitor, that he has abused your powers.
CORIOLANUS. "Traitor?" What now?
AUFIDIUS. Yes, traitor, Martius.
CORIOLANUS. Martius?

AUFIDIUS. Yes, Martius, Caius Martius. Do you think I will honor you in Corioles with that robbery, your stolen name Coriolanus? You lords and heads of the state, he has treacherously betrayed your business. For a few drops of salt water he has given up your city Rome, I say your city, to his wife and mother. He broke his oath and resolution like a thread of rotten silk. He never allowed any advice of war, but at his nurse's tears he whined and roared away your victory, so that pages blushed at him and men of heart looked at each other in wonder.
CORIOLANUS. Do you hear, Mars?
AUFIDIUS. Do not name the god, you boy of tears.
CORIOLANUS. Ha?
AUFIDIUS. No more.

CORIOLANUS. Measureless liar, you have made my heart too big for what holds it. "Boy"? Oh slave! Pardon me, lords, it is the first time I was ever forced to scold. Your judgments, my grave lords, must give this cur the lie. And his own mind, which wears my stripes pressed upon it and must carry my beating to the grave, will join in throwing the lie back at him.
FIRST LORD. Peace, both of you, and hear me speak.

CORIOLANUS. Cut me to pieces, Volsces. Men and boys, stain all your blades on me. "Boy"? False hound! If you have written your annals truly, it is there that, like an eagle in a dovecote, I fluttered your Volscians in Corioles. I did it alone. "Boy"!
AUFIDIUS. Why, noble lords, will you be reminded of his blind luck, which was your shame, by this unholy braggart, before your own eyes and ears?
ALL CONSPIRATORS. Let him die for it.
ALL PEOPLE Tear him to pieces! Do it now! He killed my son! My daughter! He killed my cousin Marcus! He killed my father!

SECOND LORD. Peace, ho! No violence! Peace! The man is noble, and his fame wraps around this whole globe of the Earth. His last offenses against us shall have a fair hearing. Stand back, Aufidius, and do not disturb the peace.
CORIOLANUS. Oh, if I had him, with six Aufidiuses, or more, his whole tribe, to use my lawful sword on.
AUFIDIUS. Insolent villain!
ALL CONSPIRATORS. Kill, kill, kill, kill, kill him!
[_Draw the Conspirators, and kills Martius, who falls. Aufidius stands on him._]
LORDS. Hold, hold, hold, hold!
AUFIDIUS. My noble masters, hear me speak.
FIRST LORD. Oh Tullus!
SECOND LORD. You have done a deed at which valor will weep.
THIRD LORD. Do not tread on him. Masters, all be quiet. Put up your swords.

AUFIDIUS. My lords, when you come to know, as in this rage, provoked by him, you cannot, the great danger his life posed to you, you will rejoice that he is cut off like this. If it pleases your Honors to call me to your senate, I will show myself your loyal servant, or endure your heaviest censure.
FIRST LORD. Carry his body away from here, and mourn him. Let him be regarded as the most noble corpse that ever a herald followed to its urn.
SECOND LORD. His own impatience takes a great part of the blame from Aufidius. Let's make the best of it.

AUFIDIUS. My rage is gone, and I am struck with sorrow. Lift him up. Help, three of the chief soldiers. I'll be one. You there, beat the drum so that it speaks mournfully. Trail your steel pikes. Though in this city he has widowed and left childless many people, who to this hour mourn the injury, yet he shall have a noble memory. Lend a hand.
[_Exeunt, bearing the body of Martius. A dead march sounded._]
